steps.instructionText: Preheat oven to 180°C and grease a mini cake tin (4 inch).
Sieve all dry ingredients for the cake into a mixing bowl and whisk to combine.
Add wet ingredients for the cake into a separate bowl and mix to combine.
Pour the cake batter into the mini cake tin and bake for 20 minutes, or until cooked through. Remove from oven and let it cool.
While the cake is cooling, prepare the frosting by adding all frosting ingredients to a bowl and stirring to combine. Chill in the fridge for 10-15 minutes to thicken.
Once the cake has cooled and the frosting has thickened, cut the cake in half and spread Biscoff frosting between the layers.
Place the top half of the cake on and coat the entire cake with the remaining frosting.
Enjoy your creation!

notes.text: 20 min at 180°C (356°F) is exact for a 4-inch mini cake; don't judge by color — whey protein browns before it's done. Use a toothpick and pull at moist crumbs; the small mass overbakes in under 2 extra minutes.
Sieve the oat flour and protein powder together — oat flour packs and protein powder clumps. Sieving aerates both so they fold into the wet ingredients without lumps.
Don't assemble while the cake is even slightly warm — the Biscoff frosting (casein + yogurt + Biscoff spread) is thick but the Biscoff fat will soften and ooze out from between the layers.
The casein in the frosting thickens on contact with liquid — stir everything together quickly and refrigerate immediately. It can go from spreadable to stiff in 5 min if left at room temp.
The egg white only (no yolk) keeps the crumb lean; bring it to room temp before mixing or it will make the batter lumpy and uneven when poured into the 4-inch tin.

steps.instructionText: Combine all the cake ingredients in a bowl and mix well.
Pour the batter evenly into two round cake molds.
Bake at 350°F for 18 minutes, or until a toothpick inserted into the center comes out clean. Be careful not to overbake.
While the cake is baking, mix the frosting ingredients together. Once the cake is cooled, decorate it with the frosting.

notes.text: 18 minutes at 350F is the maximum, not the target — with 2 scoops whey + 300 g Greek yogurt split across two thin cake layers, they overbake fast. Pull when a toothpick reads moist crumbs; a clean toothpick means dry cake.
Divide the batter by weight between the two molds, not by eye — an uneven split means one layer overbakes while the other is still underdone.
The cream-cheese frosting must go on fully cooled layers — the 10 oz cream cheese will melt and slide on a warm cake. Cool layers completely on a rack, then chill 15 minutes before frosting.
Room-temperature Greek yogurt (both the 300 g cake portion and 6 oz frosting portion) mixes lump-free; cold yogurt leaves streaks in the batter that don't hydrate evenly and can leave gummy pockets.
Don't open the oven before 15 minutes — the 1 tsp baking soda gives this cake its rise and an early door-open can cause the center to sink before it sets.

600e56ee-abd7-49fd-be95-0def5b208e5b.description: Macro-friendly frosted protein cookie (Instagram) ingested as a crumbl base-chassis candidate. Modeled with regular AP flour (source said 'Bob's Red Mill GF flour or regular flour'); generic sweetener -> granulated Splenda; the 1 egg white = 33 g (one large white); sprinkles ('to taste') omitted so it reads as a clean unfrosted-chassis sibling to the other crumbl cookies. steps.instructionText: Mix the dry ingredients together — flour, vanilla protein, Splenda, baking powder.
Add the wet ingredients (egg, egg white, melted butter, almond milk, vanilla) to the dry and mix to a dough.
Coat your hands in flour to make the dough easier to shape; divide into 5 cookies on a lined sheet.
Bake at 350F for 10 minutes.
Allow the cookies to cool fully before frosting.
Mix the Greek yogurt, SF vanilla pudding mix, vanilla, and a dash of salt into a frosting; spread on the cooled cookies (add sprinkles to taste).

notes.text: 10 minutes at 350F is the ceiling — with 3 scoops whey in only 5 cookies, these dry out fast. Pull when the edges are just set and the centers still look slightly underdone; carryover finishes them.
The dough is thick; floured hands are essential — don't skip it. If it's too stiff to shape, work in almond milk a teaspoon at a time until it just comes together without sticking.

Don't frost until the cookies are fully cool — the Greek yogurt frosting will slide off a warm cookie and go thin. If the kitchen is warm, a 10-minute fridge chill after cooling helps the frosting set.
The SF pudding mix thickens the frosting as it sits — mix and wait 5 minutes before spreading; if it's too thick, thin with a drop of almond milk, not more yogurt.
Frosted cookies stored in the fridge firm up noticeably by day 2; let them sit at room temp 10 minutes before eating for the best texture.

payload.instructionText: Brown the butter: melt the butter in a light-colored pan over medium, swirling, until it foams, then smells nutty and the milk solids turn golden-amber (~2-3 min) - pull the instant it's amber, it goes from nutty to burnt in seconds. Off the heat, stir in the cinnamon plus a pinch each of ground ginger and nutmeg and let them bloom in the hot butter ~30 sec - this is where the speculoos 'cookie' flavor comes from (brown butter alone is nutty, not spiced). Scrape it all, including the toasty brown bits, into a small bowl and cool to barely warm.
Melt 15 g Biscoff 10-15 sec until pourable and drizzle it over the top of the batter. Drag a toothpick through in a few S-curves to marble it - swirl, don't stir it in.

Beat the fat-free cream cheese alone until smooth, then add the yogurt, blended cottage cheese, protein powder, powdered peanut butter, sweetener, vanilla, lemon, the 45 g Biscoff, the cooled browned-butter spice mixture, and the vanilla pudding mix. Sift/whisk in the AP flour smooth (no lumps) and mix just until combined - don't overwork it. Warm the bowl ~15 sec if it clumps.

payload.text: Brown butter goes from nutty-amber to acrid-burnt in seconds. Pull it the moment the milk solids are golden and it smells like toffee; if it smells sharp or the bits are black, start over - burnt butter taints the whole cake.

Bloom the cinnamon, ginger, and nutmeg in the hot butter off the heat - the spices are fat-soluble, so 30 sec in the browned butter wakes them up far more than stirring them into cold batter. Brown butter brings the nutty caramel depth; the bloomed spices are what make it actually read as Biscoff.

This batter is leaner than a classic cheesecake (fat-free cream cheese), so it sets firmer and dries out faster - do NOT overbake. Pull at a just-set center with a slight wobble; chase a fully firm center and it bakes out rubbery.
Swirl the melted Biscoff on top, don't stir it in - a few toothpick S-curves keep a marbled pattern. Blend it all the way in and you just muddy the color and lose the 'Biscoff cheesecake' look.

Crustless by design - the Biscoff and browned butter carry the cookie flavor without a crust's calories. If you want a crust, the Protein Graham Crust sub-recipe slots in like it does on the other cheesecakes (about +50 cal/slice).

Blend the cottage cheese completely smooth (immersion blender or food processor) - no visible curd, or the cheesecake turns grainy.

d3a776ff-87a0-49ae-8238-0cb4a17f8ac0.description: Biscoff cookie-butter protein cheesecake, crustless - a flavor variant of the Vanilla Protein Cheesecake base, built from pantry staples (no cookie-butter emulsion, no fat-free cream cheese, no powdered PB, no brown butter). payload.instructionText: Beat the whole egg + egg white with the brown sugar only until the sugar dissolves and it looks smooth and glossy — then STOP. Chew and the shiny top come from dissolving, not air; don't whip it to a pale ribbon.
Whisk in the neutral oil, then the Greek yogurt.
Bloom the cocoa + espresso in a small splash of warm skim milk, then stir into the batter.

Whisk the flour + protein powder + salt, then fold in to no dry streaks, then ~10–15 extra strokes to develop a little gluten for chew — still stopping before it goes very stretchy or tough. No chocolate, no cornstarch.
Stir in the Splenda; add a splash more skim milk only if stiff. Spread in the pan.
Bake at 325°F for ~18 minutes, checking from ~14. Pull at only a faint center wobble — chewy wants a touch more set than fudgy, but don't dry it out.
Whisk in the coconut oil (melted if solid), then the Greek yogurt.

payload.text: Stop beating the egg + brown sugar the moment it looks glossy and the sugar has dissolved — whipping to a pale ribbon traps air, which makes the top puff then sink and kills the chew.
Blooming the 18 g cocoa in 15 ml warm milk with the espresso deepens the chocolate flavor significantly — don't skip it or add the cocoa dry, which leaves a chalky note in a batter this lean.

The 10–15 extra fold strokes after no-dry-streaks are intentional and load-bearing for chew — they develop a little gluten. Stop before the batter goes stretchy or springy; that's the line between chewy and tough.
Start checking at 14 minutes — this is a small ~6-inch pan and 30 g protein + 25 g flour dry out quickly. Pull at a faint center wobble; a clean toothpick means overbaked on this batter.
Do not cut warm — the protein-yogurt crumb is gummy and tears when hot. Cool fully on a rack, then chill for a few hours; the texture improves dramatically overnight.

payload.instructionText: Brulee the top just before serving (the shell stays crisp only ~30 min on the cake). Dust about 1.5 tbsp (20 g) brown sugar over the cold cheesecake in a thin, even layer. BROILER METHOD: rack at the top, broiler on high; freeze the cake 15-20 min first so the sugar caramelizes before the filling warms, then broil 1-4 min, rotating, watching every second - pull the moment it is an even bubbling amber, then let it set ~1 min into a crackable glass. DRY-PAN SHARD METHOD (no broiler): melt the 20 g brown sugar in a dry nonstick pan over medium heat, swirling (do not stir) until liquid and amber, pour thin onto parchment, cool until hard, snap into shards, and stand them on top just before serving.
Make and par-bake the graham crust (see the composed crust steps below), then cool it in the pan while you make the filling. The brulee filling gets poured over this crust.
Pour the filling over the cooled par-baked graham crust. Tap on the counter to level and pop bubbles.

Pull at a slight wobble in the center (~155-160F); a fully dry pick means it's already overcooked. This lean filling (cottage cheese + yogurt + whey) turns rubbery fast past done.
For the broiler method, freeze the assembled cheesecake 15-20 min first — the cold mass slows heat transfer so the 30 g brown sugar caramelizes to amber before the filling warms and weeps.
The brûlée shell softens within ~30 min on the cake; brûlée just before serving, not hours ahead, or it turns sticky and loses the crack.

Blend the cottage cheese completely smooth (immersion blender or food processor) - no visible curd, or the cheesecake turns grainy.

Beat the light cream cheese alone until smooth, then add yogurt, blended cottage cheese, protein powder, sweetener, vanilla, lemon, and vanilla pudding mix. Sift/whisk in the AP flour smooth (no lumps) and mix just until combined — don't overwork it. Warm the bowl ~15 sec if it clumps.
Add the eggs and egg white and the cooled pumpkin. Mix just until smooth - do NOT overbeat once eggs are in (air = cracks, and we want a dense set anyway).
Pour the filling over the cooled par-baked graham crust. Tap on the counter to level and pop bubbles.

Bake at 325F for ~45 min (or 350F for ~35-40 min if you want it faster) — NO water bath; a dry bake sets it denser. Pull when the center is just set with only a slight wobble (~155-160F center), not visibly jiggly. It firms further as it cools — do not chase a fully dry center, that is where a lean cheesecake turns rubbery.
Cool: oven off and door cracked 10-20 min, then counter to room temp ~1-1.5 hr (max 2 hr out), then fridge at least 4 hr — overnight is best and gives the densest, firmest set. Best the next day.

Two finishes in the method: oven broiler (freeze first) or dry-pan caramel shards (no torch). About 184 cal/slice with the crust + bigger shell (was 140 crustless). To-make.

payload.instructionText: Melt the butter + baking chocolate (low heat or short microwave bursts). Stir in the cocoa + espresso to bloom into a paste; set aside to cool slightly.

Beat the whole egg + egg white with the brown sugar only until the sugar grit dissolves and it looks smooth and glossy — then STOP. This builds chew and the shiny top; do NOT whip it to a pale, voluminous ribbon, which aerates it and bakes up holey/cakey.
Stir the Greek yogurt into the egg mixture, then fold in the cooled chocolate mixture until uniform.
Whisk the flour + protein powder + salt, then fold in just to no dry streaks — then a few extra gentle strokes for a little chew, stopping before the batter turns smooth and stretchy. No cornstarch.
Stir in the Splenda; add a splash of skim milk only if the batter is stiff. Spread in the pan.
Bake at 325°F for ~17–18 minutes, checking from ~14. Pull at a slight center jiggle — it's fudgy-leaning, so on the early side.

payload.text: Let the melted butter + chocolate cool until just warm before adding to the eggs — pouring hot chocolate into the egg mixture scrambles it and you lose the glossy emulsion the shiny top depends on.

Stop beating the egg + egg white + brown sugar (22 g) the moment the sugar grit dissolves and the mixture looks smooth and glossy. Ribboning it pale and voluminous bakes up holey and cakey, not fudgy.
Only 15 g flour and 30 g protein here — the dry folds in fast. A few extra gentle strokes after the streaks disappear builds chew; stop the instant the batter feels smooth or starts to pull.
Start checking at 14 min, not 17 — pull the moment the edges are set and the centre has a slight wobble. A clean toothpick means overbaked; you want moist crumbs clinging. Carryover sets the centre.
Chill several hours or overnight before cutting — the fudge texture only fully sets cold. Run a knife under hot water and wipe clean between cuts for neat squares.

steps.instructionText: Preheat to 325°F (165°C) and line or grease a small ~6-inch square pan.
Melt the butter + baking chocolate (low heat or short microwave bursts). Stir in the cocoa + espresso to bloom into a paste; set aside to cool slightly.

Beat the whole egg + egg white with the brown sugar only until the sugar grit dissolves and it looks smooth and glossy — then STOP. This builds chew and the shiny top; do NOT whip it to a pale, voluminous ribbon, which aerates it and bakes up holey/cakey.

Bake at 325°F for ~17–18 minutes, checking from ~14. Pull at a slight center jiggle — it's fudgy-leaning, so on the early side.

Doneness: edges set and just pulling from the sides with a slight wobble in the center (not a liquid slosh). A toothpick should read moist crumbs clinging — a clean toothpick means overbaked. On these small protein batters, trust the jiggle over the toothpick.
Cool completely in the pan on a wire rack, undisturbed — never cut warm. The crumb sets and the protein firms as it cools; a warm one seems gummy and then comes good.

Chill a few hours or overnight — they're better the next day. Cut cold with a clean knife (for the fudgy ones, run it under hot water and wipe between cuts). Store airtight; freeze portions for longer keeping. Optional: microwave a piece 8–10 sec to soften the fat — no longer, or the protein turns rubbery.

94617511-1625-427b-8849-53bbe49480cf.description: The balanced one — derived from the Fudgy base, keeping real fudge from butter + baking chocolate but adding chew: the whole egg + an extra egg white are beaten with brown sugar until glossy (dissolved, never whipped to a ribbon), the cornstarch is dropped, and protein is doubled. 1/4 cup granulated Splenda, no added milk, baked at 325F for ~17-18 min and pulled at a slight (fudgy-leaning) jiggle. Doubling protein at flat calories pulls the ratio from the base's 16.6 down to 12.5 cal per g protein. Computed ~624 cal / 50 g protein per batch of 9; ~69 cal, 5.6P, 6.7C, 2.8F per square. Large eggs (50 g whole, 33 g white). Source: user.

steps.instructionText: Preheat to 325°F (165°C) and line or grease a small ~6-inch square pan.
Melt the butter + baking chocolate over low heat or in short microwave bursts. Stir in the cocoa + espresso powder to bloom them in the warm fat — it becomes a thick paste.

Stir in the skim milk to loosen and finish blooming; warm gently to combine. For chunky brownies, reserve 1–2 tsp of the thick paste, stir a pinch of Splenda into it, and set aside. Off the heat, cool to just warm.
Stir in the Splenda, then the Greek yogurt and vanilla.
Lightly beat the egg (no whipping — keep air out so it bakes fudgy, not cakey) and stir in last. If the base is still warm, temper first: stir a spoonful of base into the egg, then add it back.

Whisk the flour + cornstarch + protein powder + salt, then fold into the batter by hand just until no dry streaks remain — then stop. A few small lumps are fine; mixing past this develops gluten and bakes up cakey. Smooth finish: fold uniform. Chunky finish: fold in the reserved sweetened paste at the very end so it stays in pockets. Spread in the pan.
Bake at 325°F for ~18 minutes, checking from ~14. Pull at a slight center jiggle (not a liquid slosh) — it should look a touch underdone; carryover heat and cooling finish the set.

Doneness: edges set and just pulling from the sides with a slight wobble in the center (not a liquid slosh). A toothpick should read moist crumbs clinging — a clean toothpick means overbaked. On these small protein batters, trust the jiggle over the toothpick.
Cool completely in the pan on a wire rack, undisturbed — never cut warm. The crumb sets and the protein firms as it cools; a warm one seems gummy and then comes good.

Chill a few hours or overnight — they're better the next day. Cut cold with a clean knife (for the fudgy ones, run it under hot water and wipe between cuts). Store airtight; freeze portions for longer keeping. Optional: microwave a piece 8–10 sec to soften the fat — no longer, or the protein turns rubbery.

notes.text: Don't whip the egg — just break the yolk and stir it in gently. Beating in air makes the batter puff in the oven and bake cakey; keeping it still keeps it dense and fudgy.
The cocoa blooms in warm butter + baking chocolate — let the fat cool to just warm (not hot) before adding the egg in step b5, or the egg scrambles. It should feel comfortable to touch.
18 min at 325°F is the max; start checking at 14 min. Pull at a slight center jiggle — not liquid, but not fully set. The protein continues cooking off-heat and the fudgy window closes fast.
If reheating a square, microwave 8–10 sec only — any longer and the protein in the Greek yogurt turns grainy and rubbery. Pull while it still feels just warm.
Stop folding the moment no dry streaks remain; the batter is small and 15 g of protein powder makes it easy to over-develop gluten. Extra strokes bake out the fudge into a tight, cakey crumb.

steps.instructionText: Preheat oven to 350°F.
Mix bananas, eggs, Greek yogurt, and vanilla extract until smooth.
Add oat flour, almond flour, baking powder, baking soda, cinnamon, and salt. Mix until combined.
Pour the batter into a greased small baking dish.
Bake for 25–30 minutes, or until set.
Let the cake cool completely.
For the frosting: mix softened light cream cheese, nonfat Greek yogurt, vanilla protein powder, maple syrup or honey, and vanilla until smooth and creamy.
Spread the frosting over the cooled cake.
Slice the cake into 4 servings.

notes.text: 25-30 min at 350F is the range — pull when a toothpick comes out with a few moist crumbs. The banana + yogurt batter keeps cooking after it comes out, and oat flour dries fast when overdone.
Use very ripe, spotted bananas: underripe bananas are starchy and the maple syrup in the frosting will be the only sweetness, leaving the cake flat.
The cream cheese must be fully softened before mixing the frosting — cold cream cheese from the fridge leaves lumps that protein powder and yogurt can't smooth out.
Don't frost until the cake is fully cool — warm cake melts the cream-cheese frosting and it slides off rather than setting into a spreadable layer.
Fold the dry into the wet gently — overmixing oat and almond flour develops a gummy texture, and with whey powder in the batter there's no gluten network to save it.

steps.instructionText: Prepare the carrots by grating them.
In a large bowl, combine the grated carrots, nonfat Greek yogurt, egg, protein powder, banana, baking powder, cinnamon, vanilla, and sweetener.
Mix all ingredients thoroughly until well combined.
Pour the batter into a prepared baking dish or individual ramekins.
Bake in a preheated oven at 180°C (350°F) for 30 minutes, or until a toothpick inserted into the center comes out clean.
Let the cake cool slightly before serving.

notes.text: 30 min at 180°C is the target for the full baking dish — individual ramekins will be done in 18–22 min. A toothpick that comes out clean is the real signal; pulling by time alone risks a dry, rubbery crumb from the 2 scoops of whey.

Add the baking soda and ACV (1 tsp) directly to the wet bowl rather than pre-mixing with dry — they need to react in the batter to give this no-flour cake its lift; mixing soda into the dry first kills that reaction.
Grate carrots fine, not coarse — coarse shreds in a low-fat, egg-light batter stay hard and don't integrate; fine grating releases moisture that helps bind the 2-scoop protein load.
"Cool slightly" isn't enough — this cake has no fat and 2 scoops of whey; cut while warm and it tears and falls apart. Cool at least 15 min, or fully to room temp for clean slices.
The 75 g banana is doing double duty as binder and natural sweetener alongside Splenda — use a ripe (spotted) banana; underripe banana adds starch without sweetness and throws off the balance.

steps.instructionText: Preheat oven to 350°F (175°C). Line an 8x8 inch baking pan with parchment paper.
For the brownie layer: In a large bowl, whisk together pumpkin purée, Greek yogurt, egg, egg whites, almond milk, and vanilla extract.
In a separate bowl, whisk together chocolate protein powder, cocoa powder, self-rising flour, sweetener, and salt.
Add the dry ingredients to the wet ingredients and mix until just combined. Do not overmix.
Spread the brownie batter evenly into the prepared baking pan.
For the cheesecake filling: In a medium bowl, beat together cream cheese, Greek yogurt, protein powder, egg, sweetener, and vanilla extract until smooth.
Carefully spoon the cheesecake filling over the brownie batter.
Bake for 25-30 minutes, or until the cheesecake is set. Let cool completely.
For the stovetop caramel topping: In a small saucepan, combine sugar-free caramel syrup, almond milk, sweetener, cornstarch, and sea salt.
Whisk constantly over medium heat until the mixture thickens, about 5-7 minutes. Remove from heat.
Pour the caramel topping over the cooled cheesecake layer and spread evenly.
Chill for at least 1 hour to set before cutting into bars.

slots.name: Torani sugar-free caramel syrup (or other brand)

notes.text: "Just combined" is critical here — this brownie layer has chocolate protein + cocoa + Greek yogurt + egg whites, all of which tighten fast when overmixed. Stop as soon as no dry flour streaks remain.
Bring the cream cheese and Greek yogurt to room temp before beating the cheesecake layer — cold dairy makes a lumpy filling that won't smooth out, and the lumps bake in permanently.
Don't beat air into the cheesecake layer — mix on low just until smooth. Airy cheesecake puffs in the oven, then cracks and sinks as it cools.

25–30 min is the window; pull when the cheesecake center has a slight wobble but isn't liquid — protein + Greek yogurt dry out fast past this point. The bars firm up fully only after cooling completely.

The Splenda-thickened caramel relies on cornstarch, not caramelization — if it's not thickening at 5 min, raise heat slightly and keep whisking. Stopping early leaves a watery sauce that soaks into the cheesecake.
Chill the full 1 hour before cutting — warm protein cheesecake is gummy and tears. For the cleanest slices, refrigerate overnight and run a warm dry knife between each cut.

payload.instructionText: Toast 65 g shredded coconut in a dry skillet over medium heat, 3-5 min, stirring, until golden and fragrant (it colors fast then burns - watch it). Cool. Grind 45 g to a fine meal (spice grinder or food processor) and beat it into the filling with the wet ingredients in step 3 so the coconut disperses throughout; reserve the other 20 g for the topping.
Once the cheesecake is fully chilled, scatter the reserved 20 g toasted coconut evenly over the top just before serving (keeps it crisp).

payload.text: Shredded coconut goes from golden to burnt in under a minute — use medium heat and stir constantly; pull the skillet off the heat the moment it smells fragrant, as residual pan heat will darken it another shade.
Once the 2 eggs and egg white go in, mix on low just until smooth — overbeating whips in air that makes the cheesecake puff, crack, and sink, and with a lean cottage-cheese base it also turns grainy.

Grind the 45 g filling coconut to a fine meal (spice grinder, 15–20 sec) before beating it in — coarse shreds leave sandy pockets; a fine meal disperses evenly and gives a smooth coconut flavor throughout every bite.

Pull at 155–160F center or when there's only a slight wobble in the middle — chasing a fully set center with 2 scoops of protein powder and cottage cheese will result in a dry, rubbery slice. It firms dramatically overnight in the fridge.
Add the 20 g toasted topping right before serving, not before refrigerating — coconut absorbs moisture in the fridge and loses its crunch within a few hours of contact with the cheesecake surface.

Grind the 45 g filling coconut to a fine meal (spice grinder, 15–20 sec) before beating it in — coarse shreds leave sandy pockets; a fine meal disperses evenly and gives a smooth coconut flavor throughout every bite.

Pull at 155–160F center or when there's only a slight wobble in the middle — chasing a fully set center with 2 scoops of protein powder and cottage cheese will result in a dry, rubbery slice. It firms dramatically overnight in the fridge.
Add the 20 g toasted topping right before serving, not before refrigerating — coconut absorbs moisture in the fridge and loses its crunch within a few hours of contact with the cheesecake surface.

steps.instructionText: Preheat oven to 180°C and grease a mini cake tin (4 inch).
Sieve all dry ingredients for the cake into a mixing bowl and whisk to combine.
Add wet ingredients for the cake into a separate bowl and mix to combine.
Pour the cake batter into the mini cake tin and bake for 20 minutes, or until cooked through. Remove from oven and let it cool.
While the cake is cooling, prepare the frosting by adding all frosting ingredients to a bowl and stirring to combine. Chill in the fridge for 10-15 minutes to thicken.
Once the cake has cooled and the frosting has thickened, cut the cake in half and spread Biscoff frosting between the layers.
Place the top half of the cake on and coat the entire cake with the remaining frosting.
Enjoy your creation!

notes.text: 20 min at 180°C (356°F) is exact for a 4-inch mini cake; don't judge by color — whey protein browns before it's done. Use a toothpick and pull at moist crumbs; the small mass overbakes in under 2 extra minutes.
Sieve the oat flour and protein powder together — oat flour packs and protein powder clumps. Sieving aerates both so they fold into the wet ingredients without lumps.
Don't assemble while the cake is even slightly warm — the Biscoff frosting (casein + yogurt + Biscoff spread) is thick but the Biscoff fat will soften and ooze out from between the layers.
The casein in the frosting thickens on contact with liquid — stir everything together quickly and refrigerate immediately. It can go from spreadable to stiff in 5 min if left at room temp.
The egg white only (no yolk) keeps the crumb lean; bring it to room temp before mixing or it will make the batter lumpy and uneven when poured into the 4-inch tin.

15a57701-be93-420b-bd69-a967f9e4ef35.description: Base protein cheesecake (vanilla SF pudding, pumpkin for moisture/body). Launch point for flavor variants. Low-fat / high-protein; pumpkin does the work fat does in a standard cheesecake. Stays lean; if a bake comes out rubbery rather than densely creamy, add a little fat (more cream cheese or an extra yolk).

payload.instructionText: Brown the butter: melt the butter in a light-colored pan over medium, swirling, until it foams, then smells nutty and the milk solids turn golden-amber (~2-3 min) - pull the instant it's amber, it goes from nutty to burnt in seconds. Off the heat, stir in the cinnamon plus a pinch each of ground ginger and nutmeg and let them bloom in the hot butter ~30 sec - this is where the speculoos 'cookie' flavor comes from (brown butter alone is nutty, not spiced). Scrape it all, including the toasty brown bits, into a small bowl and cool to barely warm.
Melt 15 g Biscoff 10-15 sec until pourable and drizzle it over the top of the batter. Drag a toothpick through in a few S-curves to marble it - swirl, don't stir it in.

Beat the fat-free cream cheese alone until smooth, then add the yogurt, blended cottage cheese, protein powder, powdered peanut butter, sweetener, vanilla, lemon, the 45 g Biscoff, the cooled browned-butter spice mixture, and the vanilla pudding mix. Sift/whisk in the AP flour smooth (no lumps) and mix just until combined - don't overwork it. Warm the bowl ~15 sec if it clumps.

payload.text: Brown butter goes from nutty-amber to acrid-burnt in seconds. Pull it the moment the milk solids are golden and it smells like toffee; if it smells sharp or the bits are black, start over - burnt butter taints the whole cake.

Bloom the cinnamon, ginger, and nutmeg in the hot butter off the heat - the spices are fat-soluble, so 30 sec in the browned butter wakes them up far more than stirring them into cold batter. Brown butter brings the nutty caramel depth; the bloomed spices are what make it actually read as Biscoff.

This batter is leaner than a classic cheesecake (fat-free cream cheese), so it sets firmer and dries out faster - do NOT overbake. Pull at a just-set center with a slight wobble; chase a fully firm center and it bakes out rubbery.
Swirl the melted Biscoff on top, don't stir it in - a few toothpick S-curves keep a marbled pattern. Blend it all the way in and you just muddy the color and lose the 'Biscoff cheesecake' look.

Crustless by design - the Biscoff and browned butter carry the cookie flavor without a crust's calories. If you want a crust, the Protein Graham Crust sub-recipe slots in like it does on the other cheesecakes (about +50 cal/slice).

Finish with the Biscoff glaze: warm all 55 g Biscoff ~20-25 sec until smooth and pourable, pour it onto the center of the fully cooled cheesecake, and tilt the pan (or use an offset spatula) to self-level it into a smooth, glossy mirror over the whole top. All 55 g of Biscoff goes on top as an unbaked glaze - undiluted and never baked, so the flavor reads far stronger and the top stays glossy (baking the spread into the batter is what muddied the look and dulled the flavor before). Press the graham crumbs on while the glaze is still tacky, not after it sets, or they won't stick - a thin ring around just the rim frames the glossy top. For an on-theme version, use crushed Biscoff cookies instead of graham.

steps.instructionText: Cook the pumpkin in a nonstick pan over medium heat, 3-5 min, stirring, until thickened and nutty. Remove and COOL COMPLETELY (hot mix will scramble the eggs).
Blend the cottage cheese completely smooth (immersion blender or food processor) - no visible curd, or the cheesecake turns grainy.

Beat the light cream cheese alone until smooth, then add the yogurt, blended cottage cheese, protein powder, sweetener, vanilla, lemon, the toasted cinnamon (toast it in a dry pan 30-60 sec until fragrant first), a pinch each of ground ginger and nutmeg, and the vanilla pudding mix. Sift/whisk in the AP flour smooth (no lumps) and mix just until combined - don't overwork it. Warm the bowl ~15 sec if it clumps.
Add the eggs and egg white and the cooled pumpkin. Mix just until smooth - do NOT overbeat once eggs are in (air = cracks, and we want a dense set anyway).
Pour into a parchment-lined 9-inch pan. Tap on the counter to level and pop bubbles.

Bake at 325F for ~45 min (or 350F for ~35-40 min if you want it faster) — NO water bath; a dry bake sets it denser. Pull when the center is just set with only a slight wobble (~155-160F center), not visibly jiggly. It firms further as it cools — do not chase a fully dry center, that is where a lean cheesecake turns rubbery.

Cool to room temp: oven off and door cracked 10-20 min (the gradual drop prevents surface cracks), then onto the counter ~1-1.5 hr until no longer warm (max 2 hr out). Don't move it to the fridge while still warm. Glaze it next, before the long chill.

Finish with the Biscoff glaze: warm all 55 g Biscoff ~20-25 sec until smooth and pourable, pour it onto the center of the fully cooled cheesecake, and tilt the pan (or use an offset spatula) to self-level it into a smooth, glossy mirror over the whole top. While the glaze is still tacky, press a ring of graham crumbs around the top edge. Then fridge at least 4 hr - overnight is best and sets the glaze to a soft, fudgy layer. Best the next day.

notes.text: The cooked pumpkin must be at room temperature before it goes in - even slightly warm, it starts cooking the eggs and leaves scrambled streaks in the finished cheesecake.
Blend the cottage cheese completely smooth - any visible curd survives baking and turns the cheesecake grainy. An immersion blender in a tall cup works; a food processor needs a full 2 minutes.

Toast the ground cinnamon in a dry pan 30-60 sec until fragrant before it goes in - straight from the jar it tastes flat; toasting blooms its oils and is what makes the spice read as speculoos against the Biscoff. Stir the ginger and nutmeg pinches in off the heat.
Don't overbeat once the eggs are in - mix on low just until smooth. Beating in air makes a lean cheesecake puff, then crack and sink, and it won't set to the dense texture this is tuned for.
A protein cheesecake sets firmer and dries out faster than a full-fat one - do NOT overbake. Pull at a just-set center with a slight wobble; chase a fully firm center and it bakes out rubbery.

Crustless by design - the Biscoff and toasted spices carry the cookie flavor without a crust's calories. If you want a crust, the Protein Graham Crust sub-recipe slots in like it does on the other cheesecakes (about +50 cal/slice).

Glaze only once the cheesecake is fully cooled - pour Biscoff onto a warm cake and it melts into the surface and slides off instead of setting as a clean mirror. Warm the spread just to pourable; over-melting makes it too thin to hold a layer, and it firms back up in the fridge.

All 55 g of Biscoff goes on top as an unbaked glaze - undiluted and never baked, so the flavor reads far stronger and the top stays glossy (baking the spread into the batter is what muddied the look and dulled the flavor before). The batter carries the speculoos spice (toasted cinnamon + ginger + nutmeg) on its own, so the bite is spiced-creamy under an intense Biscoff top.

Press the graham crumbs on while the glaze is still tacky, not after it sets, or they won't stick - a thin ring around just the rim frames the glossy top. For an on-theme version, use crushed Biscoff cookies instead of graham.

c39c0cc7-aca3-4394-b5a8-29f4c0011ed5.description: Biscoff cookie-butter protein cheesecake, crustless - a flavor variant of the Vanilla Protein Cheesecake base, built from pantry staples (no cookie-butter emulsion, no fat-free cream cheese, no powdered PB, no brown butter). Keeps the base's PROVEN dairy ratio (light cream cheese 113 g + cottage 57 g + egg white 33 g - the same ratio as the excellent-rated Creme Brulee variant) for a dense, creamy set; 55 g Biscoff (40 g batter + 15 g swirl) plus a toasted speculoos spice blend (cinnamon, ginger, nutmeg) carry the cookie flavor. ~171 cal/slice, ratio ~11.7 - a bit richer than the leanest build, but texture is the point and it's still well under the Turtle (215). To-make.

payload.instructionText: Brown the butter: melt the butter in a light-colored pan over medium, swirling, until it foams, then smells nutty and the milk solids turn golden-amber (~2-3 min) - pull the instant it's amber, it goes from nutty to burnt in seconds. Off the heat, stir in the cinnamon plus a pinch each of ground ginger and nutmeg and let them bloom in the hot butter ~30 sec - this is where the speculoos 'cookie' flavor comes from (brown butter alone is nutty, not spiced). Scrape it all, including the toasty brown bits, into a small bowl and cool to barely warm.
Melt 15 g Biscoff 10-15 sec until pourable and drizzle it over the top of the batter. Drag a toothpick through in a few S-curves to marble it - swirl, don't stir it in.

Beat the fat-free cream cheese alone until smooth, then add the yogurt, blended cottage cheese, protein powder, powdered peanut butter, sweetener, vanilla, lemon, the 45 g Biscoff, the cooled browned-butter spice mixture, and the vanilla pudding mix. Sift/whisk in the AP flour smooth (no lumps) and mix just until combined - don't overwork it. Warm the bowl ~15 sec if it clumps.

payload.text: Brown butter goes from nutty-amber to acrid-burnt in seconds. Pull it the moment the milk solids are golden and it smells like toffee; if it smells sharp or the bits are black, start over - burnt butter taints the whole cake.

Bloom the cinnamon, ginger, and nutmeg in the hot butter off the heat - the spices are fat-soluble, so 30 sec in the browned butter wakes them up far more than stirring them into cold batter. Brown butter brings the nutty caramel depth; the bloomed spices are what make it actually read as Biscoff.

This batter is leaner than a classic cheesecake (fat-free cream cheese), so it sets firmer and dries out faster - do NOT overbake. Pull at a just-set center with a slight wobble; chase a fully firm center and it bakes out rubbery.
Swirl the melted Biscoff on top, don't stir it in - a few toothpick S-curves keep a marbled pattern. Blend it all the way in and you just muddy the color and lose the 'Biscoff cheesecake' look.

Crustless by design - the Biscoff and browned butter carry the cookie flavor without a crust's calories. If you want a crust, the Protein Graham Crust sub-recipe slots in like it does on the other cheesecakes (about +50 cal/slice).

93478d92-a86a-47de-a980-1a3fcf4dcf2c.description: Base protein cheesecake (vanilla SF pudding, pumpkin for moisture/body). Launch point for flavor variants. Low-fat / high-protein; pumpkin does the work fat does in a standard cheesecake. Tuned DENSE (Tier 1+2): pumpkin reduced 120->75g + 2 tbsp AP flour for a firmer set (AP because that's what's on hand — its gluten sets denser than cornstarch), baked DRY (no water bath) to a just-set center and chilled overnight — denser at near-zero macro cost (~130 cal/slice, ratio 9.1). Stays lean; if a bake comes out rubbery rather than densely creamy, add a little fat (more cream cheese or an extra yolk).

steps.instructionText: Cook the pumpkin (or unsweetened applesauce - see note) in a nonstick pan over medium heat, 3-5 min, stirring, until thickened and nutty. Remove and COOL COMPLETELY (hot mix will scramble the eggs).
Blend the cottage cheese completely smooth (immersion blender or food processor) - no visible curd, or the cheesecake turns grainy.

Beat the light cream cheese alone until smooth, then add yogurt, blended cottage cheese, protein powder, sweetener, vanilla, lemon, and vanilla pudding mix (or its no-pudding swap - see note). Sift/whisk in the AP flour smooth (no lumps) and mix just until combined - don't overwork it. Warm the bowl ~15 sec if it clumps.
Add the eggs and egg white and the cooled pumpkin. Mix just until smooth - do NOT overbeat once eggs are in (air = cracks, and we want a dense set anyway).
Pour into a parchment-lined 9-inch pan. Tap on the counter to level and pop bubbles.

Bake at 325F for ~45 min (or 350F for ~35-40 min if you want it faster) — NO water bath; a dry bake sets it denser. Pull when the center is just set with only a slight wobble (~155-160F center), not visibly jiggly. It firms further as it cools — do not chase a fully dry center, that is where a lean cheesecake turns rubbery.
Cool: oven off and door cracked 10-20 min, then counter to room temp ~1-1.5 hr (max 2 hr out), then fridge at least 4 hr — overnight is best and gives the densest, firmest set. Best the next day.

notes.text: The cooked pumpkin MUST be room temp before it goes into the batter — even slightly warm pumpkin will begin cooking the eggs in s4 and leave scrambled streaks in the finished cheesecake.

Blend the cottage cheese until completely smooth — any visible curd survives baking and makes the cheesecake grainy. An immersion blender in a tall cup works well; a food processor needs 2 full minutes.

Don't overbeat once the eggs are in — mix on low just until smooth. Beating air into a lean cheesecake causes it to puff, then crack and sink as it cools, and it won't set to the dense texture this recipe is tuned for.
Pull when the center reads 155–160F or just barely wobbles — it looks underdone but firms fully overnight. Chasing a dry, fully-set center in the oven is where this lean formula turns rubbery.
The staged cool (oven door cracked → counter → fridge) prevents the sudden temperature drop that causes surface cracking. Don't skip the oven rest or move it to the fridge while still hot.

Out of vanilla SF pudding? Don't reach for a flavored pudding (butterscotch, etc.) - its flavor tints the whole cheesecake and fights a vanilla or berry batter. And you barely need it for structure here: the 2 tbsp AP flour plus the eggs already do the set, so the pudding is mostly vanilla flavor, a little sweetness, and the creamy body its gums lend. Clean swap: ~1 tbsp cornstarch (or skip it and lean on the flour) + an extra splash of vanilla (~1/4-1/2 tsp) and a pinch more Splenda to cover what the pudding carried. Macro-trivial - the recipe of record keeps the pudding; this is just the in-a-pinch swap. (A flavored pudding is only fair where its flavor matches the variant, e.g. butterscotch in the Banana Butterscotch Cheesecake.)

Swap: unsweetened applesauce works 1:1 for the pumpkin as the fat-replacing moisture/body. Reduce it the same way (cook it down until thickened) so it doesn't loosen the batter - applesauce starts wetter and, with more sugar than pumpkin, browns and scorches faster, so keep it moving and pull it a touch sooner. It reads a little sweeter and more neutral - actually cleaner under vanilla or a berry swirl, where pumpkin's faint earthiness can muddy things; keep the pumpkin for the warm/spiced variants (biscoff, butterscotch) where that earthiness helps. Macro-trivial (~+6 cal/recipe). Recipe of record keeps pumpkin; this is the in-a-pinch / flavor-preference swap.

payload.instructionText: Brown the butter: melt the butter in a light-colored pan over medium, swirling, until it foams, then smells nutty and the milk solids turn golden-amber (~2-3 min) - pull the instant it's amber, it goes from nutty to burnt in seconds. Off the heat, stir in the cinnamon plus a pinch each of ground ginger and nutmeg and let them bloom in the hot butter ~30 sec - this is where the speculoos 'cookie' flavor comes from (brown butter alone is nutty, not spiced). Scrape it all, including the toasty brown bits, into a small bowl and cool to barely warm.
Melt 15 g Biscoff 10-15 sec until pourable and drizzle it over the top of the batter. Drag a toothpick through in a few S-curves to marble it - swirl, don't stir it in.

Beat the fat-free cream cheese alone until smooth, then add the yogurt, blended cottage cheese, protein powder, powdered peanut butter, sweetener, vanilla, lemon, the 45 g Biscoff, the cooled browned-butter spice mixture, and the vanilla pudding mix. Sift/whisk in the AP flour smooth (no lumps) and mix just until combined - don't overwork it. Warm the bowl ~15 sec if it clumps.

This batter is leaner than a classic cheesecake (fat-free cream cheese), so it sets firmer and dries out faster - do NOT overbake. Pull at a just-set center with a slight wobble; chase a fully firm center and it bakes out rubbery.

payload.instructionText: Make the swirl: simmer the mixed berries with the Splenda and cornstarch over medium heat, mashing, until jammy and thick (4-6 min). Off heat, stir in the imitation blueberry extract. Cool fully before swirling - hot jam melts streaks into the batter.

Pour about two-thirds of the batter into the parchment-lined 9-inch pan. Spoon dollops of the cooled berry swirl over it, add the rest of the batter, dollop a little more swirl on top, and drag a knife through in S-curves to marble - 3-4 passes only (over-swirling greys the batter). Tap on the counter to level and pop bubbles.

Bake in a WATER BATH at 300F (TEST): wrap the pan bottom in foil, set it inside a larger roasting pan, and pour boiling water halfway up the sides. Bake ~55-70 min until the edges are set and the center still jiggles slightly. The gentle, humid, low heat is the classic anti-crack method - if this finishes smoother and less cracked than our dry 325F bake, we roll the water bath out to the other cheesecakes.
Once fully chilled, top with a scatter of fresh or thawed mixed berries just before serving.

payload.text: Foil-wrap the pan bottom so the bath can't seep in. Water bath + 300F = slow, even set with no surface overcook, which is what prevents the dome-and-crack. This is the recipe we're using to decide whether to convert all the cheesecakes.

The imitation blueberry extract is potent - 0.5 tsp is plenty; too much reads artificial. The cornstarch keeps the swirl from weeping into the custard. Toss the topping berries in a pinch of cornstarch if they're wet.

payload.instructionText: Cook the pumpkin (or unsweetened applesauce - see note) in a nonstick pan over medium heat, 3-5 min, stirring, until thickened and nutty. Remove and COOL COMPLETELY (hot mix will scramble the eggs).

Beat the light cream cheese alone until smooth, then add yogurt, blended cottage cheese, protein powder, sweetener, vanilla, lemon, and vanilla pudding mix (or its no-pudding swap - see note). payload.text: Swap: unsweetened applesauce works 1:1 for the pumpkin (75 g) as the fat-replacing moisture/body. Reduce it the same way (cook it down until thickened) so it doesn't loosen the batter - applesauce starts wetter and, with more sugar than pumpkin, browns and scorches faster, so keep it moving and pull it a touch sooner. It reads a little sweeter and more neutral - actually cleaner under a berry swirl, where pumpkin's faint earthiness can muddy things. Macro-trivial (~+6 cal/recipe). Recipe of record keeps pumpkin; this is the in-a-pinch / flavor-preference swap.

Out of vanilla SF pudding? Don't reach for a flavored pudding (butterscotch, etc.) - its flavor tints the whole cheesecake and fights the berry. And you barely need it for structure: the 2 tbsp AP flour plus the eggs already do the set, so the pudding is mostly vanilla flavor, a little sweetness, and the creamy body its gums lend. Clean swap: ~1 tbsp cornstarch (~8 g; or skip it and lean on the flour) + an extra splash of vanilla (~1/4-1/2 tsp) and a pinch more Splenda to cover what the pudding carried. For a berry cheesecake cornstarch is actually the cleaner pick - flavorless under the swirl. Macro-trivial; recipe of record keeps the pudding.

Pull at the first sign of a set edge with a slight wobble in the center (~155-160F) — with 2.5 scoops of protein this filling dries out faster than a traditional cheesecake. A fully still center means it's already overdone.

For a drizzle-consistency caramel (not thick), stop as soon as the almond milk is whisked smooth (~225F) and the sauce ribbons off a spoon — it thickens significantly as it cools, so pull earlier than you think you need to.

Add the almond milk WARM — cold liquid hits the melted unsweetened baking chocolate and can seize it into a grainy clump. A few seconds in the microwave before whisking it in prevents a seized ganache.

Water bath = the smooth, crack-free top, and it's the standard bake now. Foil-wrap the pan bottom and up the sides (heavy-duty, doubled) so no water seeps into the cake or crust - a slow-cooker liner bag or silicone band is extra insurance. Start with boiling water so the oven recovers temp fast. At 300F it's gentle and slow - lean on the wobble / 155-160F cue, not the clock.

eb0f7e71-16d2-4a67-84fe-94587e7f4ad5.description: Turtle protein cheesecake derived from the Vanilla Pumpkin base — pecan skipped, so caramel + chocolate carry the turtle identity. Adds a thin graham-forward chocolate crust (graham crumbs + cocoa, egg-white bound, minimal butter), a protein caramel swirl marbled into the filling (butterscotch SF pudding + 0% yogurt), and a top drizzle of REAL brown-sugar caramel + unsweetened-baking-chocolate ganache, finished with flaky salt. Filling protein bumped 2 -> 2.5 scoops to hold the macro ratio. Lands ~11.5 cal/g protein (~218 cal / 19 g protein per slice of 8). Splenda throughout, never monk fruit; the real caramel is the one honest-sugar indulgence, kept small. Bake in a 9-inch pan with a parchment sling for lift-out.

payload.instructionText: Toast 65 g shredded coconut in a dry skillet over medium heat, 3-5 min, stirring, until golden and fragrant (it colors fast then burns - watch it). Cool. Grind 45 g to a fine meal (spice grinder or food processor) and beat it into the filling with the wet ingredients in step 3 so the coconut disperses throughout; reserve the other 20 g for the topping.
Once the cheesecake is fully chilled, scatter the reserved 20 g toasted coconut evenly over the top just before serving (keeps it crisp).

payload.text: Shredded coconut goes from golden to burnt in under a minute — use medium heat and stir constantly; pull the skillet off the heat the moment it smells fragrant, as residual pan heat will darken it another shade.
Once the 2 eggs and egg white go in, mix on low just until smooth — overbeating whips in air that makes the cheesecake puff, crack, and sink, and with a lean cottage-cheese base it also turns grainy.

Grind the 45 g filling coconut to a fine meal (spice grinder, 15–20 sec) before beating it in — coarse shreds leave sandy pockets; a fine meal disperses evenly and gives a smooth coconut flavor throughout every bite.

Pull at 155–160F center or when there's only a slight wobble in the middle — chasing a fully set center with 2 scoops of protein powder and cottage cheese will result in a dry, rubbery slice. It firms dramatically overnight in the fridge.
Add the 20 g toasted topping right before serving, not before refrigerating — coconut absorbs moisture in the fridge and loses its crunch within a few hours of contact with the cheesecake surface.

payload.instructionText: Bake in a WATER BATH at 300F for ~40-45 min: foil-wrap the pan bottom and up the sides (heavy-duty, doubled) so the bath can't seep in, set it inside a larger pan, and pour boiling water halfway up the sides. The gentle, humid, low heat is the anti-crack method and gives the smooth top. Time is a guide - pull on the cue: center just set with only a slight wobble (~155-160F), not visibly jiggly. It firms further as it cools; don't chase a fully dry center, that's where a lean cheesecake turns rubbery.

payload.instructionText: Brulee the top just before serving (the shell stays crisp only ~30 min on the cake). Dust about 1.5 tbsp (20 g) brown sugar over the cold cheesecake in a thin, even layer. BROILER METHOD: rack at the top, broiler on high; freeze the cake 15-20 min first so the sugar caramelizes before the filling warms, then broil 1-4 min, rotating, watching every second - pull the moment it is an even bubbling amber, then let it set ~1 min into a crackable glass. DRY-PAN SHARD METHOD (no broiler): melt the 20 g brown sugar in a dry nonstick pan over medium heat, swirling (do not stir) until liquid and amber, pour thin onto parchment, cool until hard, snap into shards, and stand them on top just before serving.
Make and par-bake the graham crust (see the composed crust steps below), then cool it in the pan while you make the filling. The brulee filling gets poured over this crust.
Pour the filling over the cooled par-baked graham crust. Tap on the counter to level and pop bubbles.

6a37b843-9117-4026-aed1-cba3d2d3e276.description: Creme brulee cheesecake on a graham crust: vanilla custard cheesecake over a par-baked graham crust, finished with a torched brown-sugar shell. payload.instructionText: Brown the butter: melt the butter in a light-colored pan over medium, swirling, until it foams, then smells nutty and the milk solids turn golden-amber (~2-3 min) - pull the instant it's amber, it goes from nutty to burnt in seconds. Off the heat, stir in the cinnamon plus a pinch each of ground ginger and nutmeg and let them bloom in the hot butter ~30 sec - this is where the speculoos 'cookie' flavor comes from (brown butter alone is nutty, not spiced). Scrape it all, including the toasty brown bits, into a small bowl and cool to barely warm.
Melt 15 g Biscoff 10-15 sec until pourable and drizzle it over the top of the batter. Drag a toothpick through in a few S-curves to marble it - swirl, don't stir it in.

Beat the fat-free cream cheese alone until smooth, then add the yogurt, blended cottage cheese, protein powder, powdered peanut butter, sweetener, vanilla, lemon, the 45 g Biscoff, the cooled browned-butter spice mixture, and the vanilla pudding mix. Sift/whisk in the AP flour smooth (no lumps) and mix just until combined - don't overwork it. Warm the bowl ~15 sec if it clumps.

payload.text: Brown butter goes from nutty-amber to acrid-burnt in seconds. Pull it the moment the milk solids are golden and it smells like toffee; if it smells sharp or the bits are black, start over - burnt butter taints the whole cake.

Bloom the cinnamon, ginger, and nutmeg in the hot butter off the heat - the spices are fat-soluble, so 30 sec in the browned butter wakes them up far more than stirring them into cold batter. Brown butter brings the nutty caramel depth; the bloomed spices are what make it actually read as Biscoff.

This batter is leaner than a classic cheesecake (fat-free cream cheese), so it sets firmer and dries out faster - do NOT overbake. Pull at a just-set center with a slight wobble; chase a fully firm center and it bakes out rubbery.
Swirl the melted Biscoff on top, don't stir it in - a few toothpick S-curves keep a marbled pattern. Blend it all the way in and you just muddy the color and lose the 'Biscoff cheesecake' look.

Crustless by design - the Biscoff and browned butter carry the cookie flavor without a crust's calories. If you want a crust, the Protein Graham Crust sub-recipe slots in like it does on the other cheesecakes (about +50 cal/slice).

payload.text: Glaze only once the cheesecake is fully cooled - pour Biscoff onto a warm cake and it melts into the surface and slides off instead of setting as a clean mirror. Warm the spread just to pourable; over-melting makes it too thin to hold a layer, and it firms back up in the fridge.

All 55 g of Biscoff goes on top as an unbaked glaze - undiluted and never baked, so the flavor reads far stronger and the top stays glossy (baking the spread into the batter is what muddied the look and dulled the flavor before). The batter carries the speculoos spice (toasted cinnamon + ginger + nutmeg) on its own, so the bite is spiced-creamy under an intense Biscoff top.

Press the graham crumbs on while the glaze is still tacky, not after it sets, or they won't stick - a thin ring around just the rim frames the glossy top. For an on-theme version, use crushed Biscoff cookies instead of graham.

notes.text: The cooked pumpkin must be at room temperature before it goes in - even slightly warm, it starts cooking the eggs and leaves scrambled streaks in the finished cheesecake.
Blend the cottage cheese completely smooth - any visible curd survives baking and turns the cheesecake grainy. An immersion blender in a tall cup works; a food processor needs a full 2 minutes.

Toast the ground cinnamon in a dry pan 30-60 sec until fragrant before it goes in - straight from the jar it tastes flat; toasting blooms its oils and is what makes the spice read as speculoos against the Biscoff. Stir the ginger and nutmeg pinches in off the heat.
Don't overbeat once the eggs are in - mix on low just until smooth. Beating in air makes a lean cheesecake puff, then crack and sink, and it won't set to the dense texture this is tuned for.
A protein cheesecake sets firmer and dries out faster than a full-fat one - do NOT overbake. Pull at a just-set center with a slight wobble; chase a fully firm center and it bakes out rubbery.

Crustless by design - the Biscoff and toasted spices carry the cookie flavor without a crust's calories. If you want a crust, the Protein Graham Crust sub-recipe slots in like it does on the other cheesecakes (about +50 cal/slice).

Glaze only once the cheesecake is fully cooled - pour Biscoff onto a warm cake and it melts into the surface and slides off instead of setting as a clean mirror. Warm the spread just to pourable; over-melting makes it too thin to hold a layer, and it firms back up in the fridge.

Most of the Biscoff (37 g) goes on top as an unbaked glaze - undiluted and never baked, so it reads strong and stays glossy. A smaller 18 g is melted into the batter for an all-over biscoff note beneath the speculoos spice. Warm the 18 g batter Biscoff 10-15 sec until loose and pourable before it goes in - cold, stiff spread leaves streaks, and since the batter is mixed gently (to keep the dense set) you can't beat the clumps out. The 37 g topping is melted separately, just before glazing.

Water bath = the smooth, crack-free top, and it's the standard bake now. Foil-wrap the pan bottom and up the sides (heavy-duty, doubled) so no water seeps into the cake or crust - a slow-cooker liner bag or silicone band is extra insurance. Start with boiling water so the oven recovers temp fast. At 300F it's gentle and slow - lean on the wobble / 155-160F cue, not the clock.

payload.instructionText: Make the swirl: simmer the mixed berries with the Splenda and cornstarch over medium heat, mashing, until jammy and thick (4-6 min). Off heat, stir in the imitation blueberry extract. Cool fully before swirling - hot jam melts streaks into the batter.

Pour about two-thirds of the batter into the parchment-lined 9-inch pan. Spoon dollops of the cooled berry swirl over it, add the rest of the batter, dollop a little more swirl on top, and drag a knife through in S-curves to marble - 3-4 passes only (over-swirling greys the batter). Tap on the counter to level and pop bubbles.

Bake in a WATER BATH at 300F (TEST): wrap the pan bottom in foil, set it inside a larger roasting pan, and pour boiling water halfway up the sides. Bake ~55-70 min until the edges are set and the center still jiggles slightly. The gentle, humid, low heat is the classic anti-crack method - if this finishes smoother and less cracked than our dry 325F bake, we roll the water bath out to the other cheesecakes.
Once fully chilled, top with a scatter of fresh or thawed mixed berries just before serving.

payload.text: Foil-wrap the pan bottom so the bath can't seep in. Water bath + 300F = slow, even set with no surface overcook, which is what prevents the dome-and-crack. This is the recipe we're using to decide whether to convert all the cheesecakes.

The imitation blueberry extract is potent - 0.5 tsp is plenty; too much reads artificial. The cornstarch keeps the swirl from weeping into the custard. Toss the topping berries in a pinch of cornstarch if they're wet.

payload.instructionText: Cook the pumpkin (or unsweetened applesauce - see note) in a nonstick pan over medium heat, 3-5 min, stirring, until thickened and nutty. Remove and COOL COMPLETELY (hot mix will scramble the eggs).

Beat the light cream cheese alone until smooth, then add yogurt, blended cottage cheese, protein powder, sweetener, vanilla, lemon, and vanilla pudding mix (or its no-pudding swap - see note). Sift/whisk in the AP flour smooth (no lumps) and mix just until combined — don't overwork it. Warm the bowl ~15 sec if it clumps.

For a berry cheesecake cornstarch is actually the cleaner pick - flavorless under the swirl. Macro-trivial; recipe of record keeps the pudding.

Blend the cottage cheese until completely smooth — any visible curd survives baking and makes the cheesecake grainy. An immersion blender in a tall cup works well; a food processor needs 2 full minutes.

Don't overbeat once the eggs are in — mix on low just until smooth. Beating air into a lean cheesecake causes it to puff, then crack and sink as it cools, and it won't set to the dense texture this recipe is tuned for.
Pull when the center reads 155–160F or just barely wobbles — it looks underdone but firms fully overnight. Chasing a dry, fully-set center in the oven is where this lean formula turns rubbery.
The staged cool (oven door cracked → counter → fridge) prevents the sudden temperature drop that causes surface cracking. Don't skip the oven rest or move it to the fridge while still hot.

Water bath = the smooth, crack-free top, and it's the standard bake now. Foil-wrap the pan bottom and up the sides (heavy-duty, doubled) so no water seeps into the cake or crust - a slow-cooker liner bag or silicone band is extra insurance. Start with boiling water so the oven recovers temp fast. At 300F it's gentle and slow - lean on the wobble / 155-160F cue, not the clock.
The cornstarch keeps the swirl from weeping into the custard. Toss the topping berries in a pinch of cornstarch if they're wet.

Swap: unsweetened applesauce works 1:1 for the pumpkin (75 g) as the fat-replacing moisture/body. Reduce it the same way (cook it down until thickened) so it doesn't loosen the batter - applesauce starts wetter and, with more sugar than pumpkin, browns and scorches faster, so keep it moving and pull it a touch sooner. It reads a little sweeter and more neutral - actually cleaner under a berry swirl, where pumpkin's faint earthiness can muddy things. Macro-trivial (~+6 cal/recipe). Recipe of record keeps pumpkin; this is the in-a-pinch / flavor-preference swap.

Out of vanilla SF pudding? Don't reach for a flavored pudding (butterscotch, etc.) - its flavor tints the whole cheesecake and fights the berry. And you barely need it for structure: the 2 tbsp AP flour plus the eggs already do the set, so the pudding is mostly vanilla flavor, a little sweetness, and the creamy body its gums lend. Clean swap: ~1 tbsp cornstarch (~8 g; or skip it and lean on the flour) + an extra splash of vanilla (~1/4-1/2 tsp) and a pinch more Splenda to cover what the pudding carried. For a berry cheesecake cornstarch is actually the cleaner pick - flavorless under the swirl. Macro-trivial; recipe of record keeps the pudding.

The imitation blueberry extract goes into the batter, not the swirl - 0.5 tsp dispersed through the whole custard gives a slight blueberry note in every bite, while the swirl stays a pure mixed-berry ribbon. It's potent, so keep it at 0.5 tsp; more reads artificial. Add it with the wet ingredients before the flour so it distributes evenly.

If the batter is too thick to pour and swirl cleanly, thin it with a tablespoon of unsweetened almond milk (or water) at a time until it's smooth and pourable. It bakes off - the flour, pudding, and protein keep the dense set. Cold dairy or a batter that's sat a while both stiffen it, so room-temp ingredients and mixing just before you pour help too.

steps.instructionText: Preheat the oven to 350F / 175C. Line an 8x8 pan with parchment, leaving an overhang on two sides to lift the bars out later.

Brown the butter: melt it in a small light-colored pan over medium heat, swirling, until it foams, the milk solids turn golden-brown, and it smells nutty (3-5 min). Scrape it - browned bits and all - into a large bowl and let it cool a few minutes so it won't cook the egg.
Whisk the brown sugar and Splenda into the warm browned butter until glossy, then whisk in the whole egg, Greek yogurt, and vanilla until smooth and slightly fluffy.

Add the vanilla whey, butterscotch pudding mix, AP flour, baking powder, and salt. Fold just until no dry streaks remain - don't overmix. If the batter is too stiff to spread, loosen it with the almond milk a splash at a time until thick but spreadable.
Scrape into the pan and press/smooth it level - it's a thick batter, not a pourable one.

Bake at 350F for ~16-20 min. Pull it when the edges are set but the center still looks a touch underdone with a faint jiggle - it firms as it cools. UNDERBAKE on purpose: whey goes from chewy to dry within a couple minutes past this point.

Cool in the pan ~10 min, then lift out by the parchment onto a rack so the carryover stops. Cool fully before cutting into 9 squares - they set chewy as they cool, and they're even better the next day.

slots.name: brown sugar (dark if you have it)

notes.text: Browning the butter is what lets a single tablespoon read like more - it builds a nutty, caramel-adjacent depth that doubles down on the brown sugar. Take it to golden and nutty, not burnt, and pour it out as soon as it's there since it keeps cooking in the hot pan.

Real brown sugar is load-bearing here, not just sweetness: its molasses IS the butterscotch flavor, and its moisture is what keeps these soft and chewy for days. Splenda only tops up the sweetness without adding calories - don't swap the brown sugar out entirely or you lose both the flavor and the chew.

The butterscotch SF pudding stacks more butterscotch onto the brown sugar for almost no calories, and its starch/gums lend a creamy, cohesive set. Vanilla SF pudding subs fine if that's what's open - just a little less butterscotch punch.

The bake window is short and unforgiving with whey (no casein here to keep it soft) - it flips from chewy to spongy-dry within a couple minutes of done. Pull it looking slightly underbaked; carryover and cooling finish the set. A center that looks fully dry in the oven is already overbaked on the plate.

a56c28c0-e003-4051-9476-ce8f836f987a.name: Browned-Butter Butterscotch Blondie
a56c28c0-e003-4051-9476-ce8f836f987a.description: Browned-butter butterscotch blondie - dense, soft, and chewy, sitting between a fudgy brownie and a buttery cookie bar. steps.instructionText: Preheat the oven to 350F / 175C. Line an 8x8 pan with parchment, leaving an overhang on two sides to lift the bars out later.

Brown the butter: melt it in a small light-colored pan over medium heat, swirling, until it foams, the milk solids turn golden-brown, and it smells nutty (3-5 min). Scrape it - browned bits and all - into a large bowl and let it cool a few minutes so it won't cook the egg.
Whisk the brown sugar and Splenda into the warm browned butter until glossy, then whisk in the whole egg, Greek yogurt, and vanilla until smooth and slightly fluffy.

Add the vanilla whey, butterscotch pudding mix, AP flour, baking powder, and salt. Fold just until no dry streaks remain - don't overmix. If the batter is too stiff to spread, loosen it with the almond milk a splash at a time until thick but spreadable.
Scrape into the pan and press/smooth it level - it's a thick batter, not a pourable one.

Bake at 350F for ~16-20 min. Pull it when the edges are set but the center still looks a touch underdone with a faint jiggle - it firms as it cools. UNDERBAKE on purpose: whey goes from chewy to dry within a couple minutes past this point.

Cool in the pan ~10 min, then lift out by the parchment onto a rack so the carryover stops. Cool fully before cutting into 9 squares - they set chewy as they cool, and they're even better the next day.

Finish: once fully cooled and cut, drizzle the sugar-free maple syrup over the top (or over each square as you serve). Added cold and never baked, it stays glossy and reinforces the maple-butterscotch note for almost no calories.

Real brown sugar is load-bearing here, not just sweetness: its molasses IS the butterscotch flavor, and its moisture is what keeps these soft and chewy for days. Splenda only tops up the sweetness without adding calories - don't swap the brown sugar out entirely or you lose both the flavor and the chew.

3de86c81-3c59-46ac-8af0-b4fc0525523b.name: High Protein Brookie
3de86c81-3c59-46ac-8af0-b4fc0525523b.description: A baked two-layer protein brookie built on blended cottage cheese (not flour or butter): a cocoa brownie layer under a vanilla cookie layer, both leavened with baking powder, chocolate chips folded into each. Distinct from the flour-based Fudgy Protein Brownies — this is a cottage-cheese protein bake. House calibration: the COOKIE layer uses REAL brown sugar (3 tbsp) for the chew and molasses depth that define a chocolate-chip cookie; the brownie layer stays granulated Splenda (cocoa carries the flavor and it keeps that layer leaner).

steps.instructionText: Combine the chocolate protein, Splenda, blended cottage cheese, cacao, and baking powder. Fold in the chocolate chips and spread into a parchment-lined 8-inch square (8x8) pan, leveled flat.
Combine the vanilla protein, brown sugar, blended cottage cheese, vanilla, salt, and baking powder. Fold in the chocolate chips and pour over the brownie layer.

Bake at 325F (not 350) until the cookie top looks set and a pick in the center pulls out with a few moist crumbs - start checking at 30 minutes. 40-45 minutes is the outer ceiling, not a target: this is a flourless, fat-free cottage-cheese + protein batter, so it turns rubbery the instant it fully dries, and lower-and-slower sets the center before the top overshoots. Cool completely in the pan (a fridge chill helps) before slicing into 5 squares - it firms as it sets.

notes.text: Stir the brownie layer just until combined - overmixing the cottage-cheese base builds structure and you lose the fudgy density.
The cookie layer is a thick, scoopable dough; if it's too stiff to spread over the brownie, work in milk a teaspoon at a time until it just spreads. Don't thin it all the way to a batter.
45 min is the ceiling, not the target - protein + cottage cheese dry out fast. Pull when a pick in the cookie layer comes out with a few moist crumbs; the center keeps cooking as it cools.

ee6eba5b-d90e-4bbe-8ac2-0f27d2558e1d.name: Protein Tres Leches
ee6eba5b-d90e-4bbe-8ac2-0f27d2558e1d.description: A high-protein tres leches: a light protein sponge (0% Greek yogurt + egg whites + vanilla protein) baked, poked, and flooded with a vanilla-protein milk soak, then chilled until it drinks it all in. Adapted from a 1UP Tres Leches recipe — coconut flour swapped for oat flour (leaner: less fat, more carb) and finished with a cinnamon + sugar-free caramel (dulce-de-leche style) topping instead of plain whip. Uses a VANILLA / 'tres leches'-flavored protein, not chocolate.

steps.instructionText: Preheat the oven to 380F and line an 8x8 pan with parchment. Whisk the Greek yogurt, egg whites, and skim milk until smooth, then fold in the AP flour, oat flour, baking soda, vanilla protein, and cinnamon just until combined - don't overmix, protein batter turns rubbery. Spread evenly into the pan.
Bake about 18-22 minutes at 380F, until the top springs back and a toothpick comes out clean. Cool roughly 10 minutes - keep it warm for soaking.

Whisk the soak milk and vanilla protein until completely smooth and lump-free. Poke the still-warm cake all over with a skewer, right down to the bottom. Pour the leche mixture evenly over the top - it WILL pool on the surface, that's correct. Cover and refrigerate at least 4 hours, ideally overnight, until the cake drinks it all in.

Spread the whipped topping over the soaked, chilled cake, dust with cinnamon, and drizzle the sugar-free caramel generously over the top (dulce-de-leche style - the classic tres leches finish). Add sliced fresh strawberries if you like. Slice into 4 and serve cold.

notes.text: Don't overbake the sponge - a tres leches cake has to stay tender enough to drink the milk. Pull it the moment a toothpick is clean; an overbaked, dry cake repels the soak instead of absorbing it.

Poke the holes all the way to the bottom and soak while warm - a warm, poked cake wicks the leche evenly, while pouring onto a cold sealed cake leaves it sitting on top. Overnight beats 4 hours; the crumb keeps drinking as it sits.

Coconut flour (in the original) was swapped for oat flour - leaner (less fat, more carb) but far less absorbent, so the amount is bumped a touch (2 tbsp coconut -> 3 tbsp / 22 g oat) to keep the crumb sturdy enough to hold the soak. The batter will look slightly wetter than a coconut-flour version; that's expected.

Toppings are to taste: it stays leaner with a light hand of Cool Whip (most of its calories are fat). The sugar-free caramel is 0-cal, so drizzle freely - that dulce-de-leche note is what makes it read as tres leches. A pinch of cinnamon whisked into the whip is a nice touch.

Uses a VANILLA / 'tres leches'-flavored protein, NOT chocolate - chocolate would turn the whole thing into a chocolate tres leches. The original used 1UP Tres Leches; any vanilla/cake-flavored whey works.

019a4f0f-d891-43e0-b29c-1ad354ab2c0b.description: A lean, genuinely TOASTED s'mores protein brownie: a fudgy cottage-cheese + chocolate-protein brownie on a thin honey-graham base, topped with REAL mini marshmallows broiled until golden plus a light scatter of chocolate chips. steps.instructionText: Preheat to 350F and line a small loaf pan (or one quarter of an 8x8) with parchment. Mix the graham crumbs with the small amount of maple syrup until sandy, then press firmly into the bottom of the pan - this is your cracker layer.

Blend the cottage cheese completely smooth (no curds left), then mix in the chocolate protein, cocoa, oat flour, egg whites, the rest of the maple, Splenda, and baking powder until you have a smooth, thick batter. Spread it evenly over the graham base.

Bake about 18-22 minutes at 350F, until the top is set and a toothpick comes out with a few moist crumbs. Don't overbake - a cottage-cheese protein brownie dries and turns rubbery fast, so pull it while it's still fudgy. Cool a few minutes.

Scatter the mini marshmallows and chocolate chips over the top. Broil 30-60 seconds, watching the WHOLE time, until the marshmallows puff and turn golden (they go from toasted to burnt in seconds). Crush a little extra graham over if you like. Cool, then cut into 4 squares.

notes.text: Don't overbake the brownie - a fat-free cottage-cheese + protein batter has no fat or flour buffer, so it goes from fudgy to dry-and-rubbery fast. Pull it with a few moist crumbs on the pick; it firms as it cools.

Broiler marshmallows burn in SECONDS - do not walk away, do not check your phone. Watch through the door and pull the moment they're golden and puffed. A kitchen torch gives you more control if you have one.
Blend the cottage cheese totally smooth BEFORE adding the dry ingredients - any curds left will show up as little white lumps in the finished brownie.

Mini marshmallows are fat-free, so they're the one place to be generous - they carry the whole toasted-s'mores payload at zero fat cost. The graham base and chocolate chips are the only real fat in the recipe, which is why they're kept deliberately minimal (keeps it ~17% fat).

Built to replace the original Protein S'mores Brownies (492 cal, ~36% fat). Changes: dropped the coconut-oil drizzle, swapped the un-toasted yogurt/pudding 'marshmallow' frosting for REAL broiled mini marshmallows, switched to chocolate protein, and cut the batch ~in half. Result lands ~17% fat.

steps.instructionText: Preheat to 350F and line a small loaf pan (or one quarter of an 8x8) with parchment. Mix the graham crumbs with the small amount of maple syrup until sandy, then press firmly into the bottom of the pan - this is your cracker layer.

Blend the cottage cheese completely smooth (no curds left), then mix in the chocolate protein, cocoa, oat flour, egg whites, the rest of the maple, Splenda, and baking powder until you have a smooth, thick batter. Spread it evenly over the graham base.

Bake about 18-22 minutes at 350F, until the top is set and a toothpick comes out with a few moist crumbs. Don't overbake - a cottage-cheese protein brownie dries and turns rubbery fast, so pull it while it's still fudgy. Cool a few minutes.

Spoon the meringue over the FULLY COOLED brownie and swirl it into rough, spiky peaks with the back of the spoon - those peaks are what brown, so don't smooth it flat. Scatter the chocolate chips over the top.

Toast it under the broiler: (1) Move an oven rack to the TOP position, about 4-6 inches below the top heating element. (2) Set the oven to BROIL on HIGH and let it heat 3-5 minutes until that top element is glowing orange. (3) Slide the topped brownie onto the top rack, directly under the element. (4) STAY and WATCH through the door with the oven light on - in 30 to 90 seconds the meringue peaks toast and go golden-brown, tips first. (5) The second they look like a toasted marshmallow, pull it out (rotate the pan once partway if one side browns faster - broilers are uneven). Cool a few minutes, then cut into 4 squares.

The marshmallow stand-in is a torched honey-meringue (fat-free, adds protein). Lands ~17-18% fat.

New to broiling? The 'broiler' is your oven's top heating element - it fires intense heat straight DOWN to brown tops fast, like an upside-down grill. (On many gas ovens it's a pull-out drawer underneath the oven instead of a setting.) Move the rack up BEFORE you turn it on, choose the 'Broil' or 'Hi Broil' setting, and keep the door closed on a modern electric oven (only crack it if your manual says to). Use a metal pan and tuck any parchment edges down so they can't touch the element.

No broiler at all? Crank the oven to 475-500F and put the topped brownie on the top rack for 4-6 minutes, watching it the same way. Or skip toasting entirely - the meringue is still sweet and good unbrowned, just paler and without the campfire flavor.
