steps.instructionText: Preheat oven to 350°F.
Crush graham crackers and mix with maple syrup. Press this mixture onto the bottom of a 9x5 loaf pan.
Combine all brownie ingredients in a bowl and mix well. Spread this batter evenly over the graham cracker base.
Bake for approximately 45 minutes, or until a toothpick inserted into the center comes out clean. Be careful not to overbake, as this can affect the fudgy texture.
While the brownies bake, prepare the frosting by mixing all frosting ingredients together until smooth. If using pudding mix, add it to thicken the frosting.
Once the brownies have cooled slightly, spread the frosting evenly over the top.

Sprinkle crushed graham crackers over the frosting. If desired, prepare the chocolate drizzle by melting the oil and chocolate together in the microwave in 30-second intervals until smooth, then drizzle over the brownies.
Cut the brownies into four pieces to create squares. For the best texture and flavor, chill the brownies in the refrigerator before serving.

notes.text: 45 min is dangerously long for a Greek yogurt + pumpkin batter — check at 30 min. Pull when a pick reads moist crumbs; the pumpkin holds moisture but the protein still turns rubbery if pushed past set.
The graham base needs firm pressing — pack it tightly with the bottom of a measuring cup so it holds together as a layer when you pour batter on top. A loose base crumbles when you cut the squares.
The step says 'cooled slightly' but the yogurt frosting will melt and slide on a warm brownie. Wait until the pan is fully cool to the touch before spreading — at least 30 min on a rack.
For the chocolate drizzle, melt the 3 tbsp coconut oil with chocolate in 30-sec microwave bursts and stir between each — coconut oil separates quickly and scorches if microwaved all at once.
Chill before cutting — this layered brownie (graham base + pumpkin-protein body + frosting) holds together cleanly only when cold. Warm, the layers slide and the bars fall apart.

No broiler at all? Crank the oven to 475-500F and put the topped brownie on the top rack for 4-6 minutes, watching it the same way. Or skip toasting entirely - the meringue is still sweet and good unbrowned, just paler and without the campfire flavor.

Graham in two forms, each where it works best: CRUMBS for the base - bound with the maple and egg white they press into an even layer that cuts cleanly with the soft brownie and resists sogging - and whole-cracker SHARDS on top (optional) for the crisp snap, which only survives up top where it isn't buried in wet batter. Don't line the base with whole wafers: they crack when you slice and go soft by day two.

Reading meringue peaks: lift the beaters straight out. SOFT peaks flop over at the tip; STIFF peaks stand straight up and hold. Stiff, glossy peaks are ideal for a broiled topping - they hold the spiky swirls that brown best - but soft-to-medium peaks also work fine (made and rated excellent that way): they just spread a little flatter and brown more evenly instead of in spikes. So don't kill yourself chasing stiff, especially with pasteurized whites; just get it past the loose, ribbony stage. Whatever you reach, stop while it's still glossy - beat past that and the foam goes dry, dull and grainy and beads water in the oven.

By hand (no mixer): use a BALLOON WHISK, not a spatula - a spatula folds air out, so it can't build a meringue. The bowl and whisk must be spotlessly grease-free (metal or glass beats plastic; a speck of fat or yolk kills the foam), and room-temp whites plus the cream of tartar both help it stiffen faster. Expect about 5-8 minutes of brisk, near-continuous whisking to reach stiff peaks for this small amount - LONGER if your whites are carton/pasteurized; soft peaks arrive around 3-4 minutes, push past them. Add the real sugar gradually (dumping it all at once deflates the foam and takes longer to recover). Use a spatula or spoon only afterward, to scrape the meringue out and swirl it onto the brownie.

Egg whites: FRESH shell whites whip fastest and highest. CARTON / pasteurized whites work, but the pasteurization heat partially sets the proteins, so they whip slower, with more effort, and may not get quite as stiff - lean on the acid and be patient (the warm-bowl Swiss method helps a lot here). On acid: one pinch of cream of tartar per ~2 whites is the FULL dose - it lowers the pH so the foam forms and holds. More won't whip it faster (the holdup is mechanical) and won't taste sour at this level, but don't pile it on. Prefer dry cream of tartar over lemon juice - lemon adds water that slackens the foam; if it's all you have, a few drops is plenty.

A pinch of instant espresso (about 1/8 tsp) amplifies the cocoa so the brownie tastes MORE chocolatey, not like coffee - but keep it to a pinch. Too much tips it toward mocha/coffee. (Tested: a little over a pinch still tasted excellent, but a pinch is the target.)

steps.instructionText: Preheat to 350F and line an 8x4-inch loaf pan (or any small pan about 1 inch / 2.5 cm deep) with parchment. Stir the graham crumbs together with the maple syrup AND the egg whites until evenly moistened (like wet sand), then press firmly and evenly into the bottom of the pan - this is your cracker layer. The egg white sets as it bakes, gluing the crumbs into a firm crust that cuts cleanly with the brownie instead of crumbling apart.

Blend the cottage cheese completely smooth (no curds left), then mix in the chocolate protein, cocoa, oat flour, egg whites, the rest of the maple, Splenda, baking powder, and a pinch of instant espresso (about 1/8 tsp - it deepens the chocolate without tasting like coffee) until you have a smooth, thick batter. Spread it evenly over the graham base.

Bake at 350F, about 16-20 minutes - start checking at 14. Pull it when the top looks set and a pick in the center comes out with a few moist crumbs (not wet batter, but not bone-dry). This fat-free cottage-cheese + protein batter dries and turns rubbery fast, so err on the early side; it keeps firming as it cools. Cool it FULLY before topping, or the warm meringue will slide off.

Make the meringue (your marshmallow stand-in) by whipping the whites through three stages - aim for STIFF peaks, passing through the first two on the way: (1) FOAMY - whip the egg whites (add a pinch of cream of tartar - or a few drops of lemon juice/vinegar - especially if your whites are the carton/pasteurized kind) on medium until white and frothy with small bubbles, like loose bubble bath, with no real structure yet. This is your cue to start adding sugar. (2) SOFT PEAKS - with the beaters running, rain in the granulated sugar a little at a time (about a teaspoon every 10-15 seconds); soon, when you lift the beaters, a peak forms but its tip flops over. Keep whipping. (3) STIFF PEAKS (your target) - keep going until you lift the beaters straight up and the peak stands on its own without the tip folding and the meringue looks thick and glossy, then beat in the Splenda for just a few seconds at the very end (it's only for sweetness; added early it doesn't dissolve and can slow the foam). STOP once stiff and glossy. Don't whip past glossy: if it turns dull, dry, or grainy/curdled you've gone too far and it will weep in the oven. Rub a dab between two fingers - it should feel smooth, not gritty; if it's gritty the sugar hasn't dissolved, so keep whipping a touch.

Spoon the meringue over the FULLY COOLED brownie and swirl it into rough, spiky peaks with the back of the spoon - those peaks are what brown, so don't smooth it flat. Scatter the chocolate chips over the top. Optional, if you have whole graham crackers: break a few into shards and scatter them on too - up here by the 'marshmallow' they keep the crisp graham SNAP of a real s'more (down in the base they'd just go soggy).

Toast it under the broiler: (1) Move an oven rack to the TOP position, about 4-6 inches below the top heating element. (2) Set the oven to BROIL on HIGH and let it heat 3-5 minutes until that top element is glowing orange. (3) Slide the topped brownie onto the top rack, directly under the element. (4) STAY and WATCH through the door with the oven light on - in 30 to 90 seconds the meringue peaks toast and go golden-brown, tips first. (5) The second they look like a toasted marshmallow, pull it out (rotate the pan once partway if one side browns faster - broilers are uneven). Cool a few minutes, then cut into 4 squares.

notes.text: Don't overbake the brownie - with almost no fat and only a little oat flour to buffer it, a cottage-cheese + protein batter goes from fudgy to dry-and-rubbery fast. Pull it with a few moist crumbs on the pick; it firms as it cools.
The broiler goes from golden to BURNT in seconds and it is blazing hot - never walk away or check your phone. Watch the whole time and pull the instant the peaks are golden.
Blend the cottage cheese totally smooth BEFORE adding the dry ingredients - any curds left will show up as little white lumps in the finished brownie.

8c8821f6-d7f2-49b3-aafc-a3ed745ca61f.name: Browned-Butter Protein Cookies (Oat Flour)
8c8821f6-d7f2-49b3-aafc-a3ed745ca61f.author: user
8c8821f6-d7f2-49b3-aafc-a3ed745ca61f.commitMessage: derive variant from Browned-Butter Protein Cookies (60g protein)

steps.instructionText: Brown the butter: melt it in a pan over medium heat, swirling, until golden and nutty-smelling (3-4 min). Pour into a mixing bowl and let cool a couple minutes so it won't cook the egg.
Mix wet: whisk in the brown sugar, Splenda, whole egg, egg white, and vanilla until smooth and glossy. Don't whip air in - just combine.

Add dry: stir in the whey, flour, pudding mix, baking soda, and salt until a thick, scoopable dough forms, then fold in the chocolate chips. It should hold its shape, not pour. Too stiff/dry -> a splash of milk; too loose -> a bit more flour. Taste for sweetness.
Chill the dough 30 minutes.
Shape into 3 tall mounds - do NOT flatten.

Bake at 330°F / 165°C - start checking at ~10 minutes to be safe (they may take up to ~15 depending on your oven). Pull when the edges are set but the center still looks slightly underdone/soft - they stay pale, so don't wait for golden tops. Optional, for flatter, chewier cookies with crinkly tops: partway through (around the 6–7 min mark) slide the tray out and rap it firmly on the counter once or twice to deflate and spread the mounds (and again right out of the oven); skip it to keep them thick and domed.
Rest: leave the cookies on the hot tray 10-15 min after baking - they finish cooking from residual heat and firm up from floppy to chewy as they cool. Don't judge texture until fully cooled.
Fridge (optional): for a firmer, denser, chewier bite, refrigerate the cooled cookies 20-30 min or longer. Protein cookies tighten up when cold. Store leftovers in the fridge.

notes.text: Let the browned butter cool a couple minutes before adding eggs — 60 g of whey is already heat-sensitive; scrambled egg in the fat ruins the emulsion and makes the cookie grainy.
60 g whey is a heavy protein load for 3 cookies; add milk a teaspoon at a time only if the dough won't come together — too much liquid makes it spread flat and bake rubbery.

These stay pale - Splenda doesn't brown. Start checking at ~10 min and pull once the edges are just set and the center still looks underdone; waiting for any color (or the full 15 min) risks overbaked, dry centers.
The 10–15 min pan rest is where the centers finish cooking and proteins set. Moving them too soon means they fall apart; judging texture before fully cooled gives a false "gummy" read.
The 30-min chill firms the butter so the mounds hold their height and spread slowly — skip it and 60 g of whey in a small yield will spread flat and bake through before centers can stay gooey.

The optional pan-slap is the bakery 'pan-bang' trick: dropping the hot tray collapses the risen center so the cookie spreads thin with crackly, rippled edges and a chewier bite. Do it halfway and again out of the oven for the most spread; skip it entirely to keep these tall and gooey.

Super chocolatey, melt in the mouth fudge, so good you could easily devour them all. a4280dbe-3455-4cc3-becd-878caf7a62ad.commitMessage: Fix import artifacts: glaze protein vanilla->chocolate (match the recipe); glaze milk '1 each'(=244g, would never set) -> 1 tbsp; re-pin glaze ingredients to step 5 and melted chocolate to step 2; add body/glaze sections

steps.instructionText: Blend all the base ingredients except the melted chocolate (the glaze is made separately in the final step).
Pour in melted chocolate and blend briefly or fold through until smooth.
Add a splash of milk if needed to loosen slightly (should be thick but spreadable).
Spread into a lined container and smooth the top.
Mix the glaze ingredients and pour over the top. Sprinkle with flaky sea salt.
Chill in the fridge for 1–2 hours until firm.
Slice into 9 squares.

notes.text: Blend the 300 g cottage cheese until completely smooth before adding the other ingredients — any remaining curds create a grainy fudge texture that no amount of chilling will fix.
Make sure the melted chocolate has cooled slightly before blending it in — hot chocolate can seize or separate when it hits cold cottage cheese, giving a greasy, split texture.
Add milk a tiny splash at a time — the almond flour and 60 g protein make this mixture look stiffer than it is. Over-thinning produces bars that never set firm, even after 2 hours in the fridge.
Warm the chocolate-hazelnut spread (glaze) for 10–15 seconds so it pours easily and levels itself — unwarmed it drags the protein base underneath and creates an uneven top.
1–2 hours in the fridge is the minimum; these are much better after 3–4 hours and easiest to slice cleanly when cut cold. Temper a square 3–5 minutes at room temp before eating if they set rock-hard.

f820dd6f-663b-4bda-bdc8-947fa081d6b8.name: Peanut Caramel Protein Twix Bars
f820dd6f-663b-4bda-bdc8-947fa081d6b8.description: A protein Twix: baked shortbread-style base, a real brown-sugar peanut caramel, and a thin chocolate shell. Adapted from a PB-powder-based protein twix — rebuilt without peanut-butter powder (not on hand) and leaned caramel-forward (caramel > PB > chocolate) for better macros. Subs: unflavored plant protein -> plain whey isolate; vanilla whey-casein -> vanilla whey; the PB-powder 'caramel' -> an actual brown-sugar + Fairlife caramel with a modest amount of real creamy PB; SF chopped chocolate -> semi-sweet chips (no SF chocolate in the library), trimmed thin. House calibration: real brown sugar in the caramel (molasses matters); Splenda for added sweetness elsewhere.
f820dd6f-663b-4bda-bdc8-947fa081d6b8.author: user

steps.instructionText: Base: whisk together the oat flour, plain whey isolate, vanilla whey, coconut flour, and Splenda.
Stir in the almond milk to form a stiff, pressable dough. Press firmly and evenly into a parchment-lined loaf pan or small square pan.
Bake at 325 F (160 C) for 10-12 minutes, until just set and dry to the touch. Cool completely before adding the caramel.
Peanut caramel: in a small saucepan over low heat, stir the brown sugar, Fairlife milk, and salt until dissolved and slightly thickened, 3-4 minutes.
Off the heat, stir in the peanut butter until smooth, then the vanilla whey. Spread over the cooled base and chill until set, ~30 minutes.
Chocolate shell: melt the chocolate chips with the coconut oil (short microwave bursts, stirring) and spread in a thin even layer over the caramel.
Chill until the chocolate is set, then lift out and slice into 8 bars. Cut cold for clean edges.

notes.text: Don't overbake the base — pull it as soon as it's set and dry on top. Overbaked, it turns rock-hard and the bars shatter instead of giving a clean twix-style snap.
Stir the vanilla whey into the caramel OFF the heat — protein powder added to a hot, actively-boiling caramel clumps and turns grainy. Take the pan off, let it stop bubbling, then stir it in.
The peanut butter is the main fat in the whole bar (everything else is lean). Don't add more than the 22 g — extra PB both blows the fat budget and softens the caramel so it won't set firm.
Chill the caramel layer firm BEFORE pouring the chocolate, or the warm chocolate melts into it and you lose the distinct twix layers.
Caramel-forward by design (caramel > PB > chocolate). To push it even more caramel-heavy, bump the brown sugar — it's fat-free, so it adds caramel flavor and carbs without touching the fat budget.

steps.instructionText: Preheat to 350F and line an 8x4-inch loaf pan (or any small pan about 1 inch / 2.5 cm deep) with parchment. Stir the graham crumbs together with the maple syrup AND the egg whites until evenly moistened (like wet sand), then press firmly and evenly into the bottom of the pan - this is your cracker layer. The egg white sets as it bakes, gluing the crumbs into a firm crust that cuts cleanly with the brownie instead of crumbling apart.

Blend the cottage cheese completely smooth (no curds left), then mix in the chocolate protein, cocoa, oat flour, egg whites, the rest of the maple, Splenda, baking powder, and a pinch of instant espresso (about 1/8 tsp - it deepens the chocolate without tasting like coffee) until you have a smooth, thick batter. Spread it evenly over the graham base.

Bake at 350F, about 16-20 minutes - start checking at 14. Pull it when the top looks set and a pick in the center comes out with a few moist crumbs (not wet batter, but not bone-dry). This fat-free cottage-cheese + protein batter dries and turns rubbery fast, so err on the early side; it keeps firming as it cools. Cool it FULLY before topping, or the warm meringue will slide off.

Make the meringue (your marshmallow stand-in) by whipping the whites through three stages - aim for STIFF peaks, passing through the first two on the way: (1) FOAMY - whip the egg whites (add a pinch of cream of tartar - or a few drops of lemon juice/vinegar - especially if your whites are the carton/pasteurized kind) on medium until white and frothy with small bubbles, like loose bubble bath, with no real structure yet. This is your cue to start adding sugar. (2) SOFT PEAKS - with the beaters running, rain in the granulated sugar a little at a time (about a teaspoon every 10-15 seconds); soon, when you lift the beaters, a peak forms but its tip flops over. Keep whipping. (3) STIFF PEAKS (your target) - keep going until you lift the beaters straight up and the peak stands on its own without the tip folding and the meringue looks thick and glossy, then beat in the Splenda for just a few seconds at the very end (it's only for sweetness; added early it doesn't dissolve and can slow the foam). STOP once stiff and glossy. Don't whip past glossy: if it turns dull, dry, or grainy/curdled you've gone too far and it will weep in the oven. Rub a dab between two fingers - it should feel smooth, not gritty; if it's gritty the sugar hasn't dissolved, so keep whipping a touch.

Spoon the meringue over the FULLY COOLED brownie and swirl it into rough, spiky peaks with the back of the spoon - those peaks are what brown, so don't smooth it flat. Scatter the chocolate chips over the top. Optional, if you have whole graham crackers: break a few into shards and scatter them on too - up here by the 'marshmallow' they keep the crisp graham SNAP of a real s'more (down in the base they'd just go soggy).

Toast it under the broiler: (1) Move an oven rack to the TOP position, about 4-6 inches below the top heating element. (2) Set the oven to BROIL on HIGH and let it heat 3-5 minutes until that top element is glowing orange. (3) Slide the topped brownie onto the top rack, directly under the element. (4) STAY and WATCH through the door with the oven light on - in 30 to 90 seconds the meringue peaks toast and go golden-brown, tips first. (5) The second they look like a toasted marshmallow, pull it out (rotate the pan once partway if one side browns faster - broilers are uneven). Cool a few minutes, then cut into 4 squares.

notes.text: Don't overbake the brownie - with almost no fat and only a little oat flour to buffer it, a cottage-cheese + protein batter goes from fudgy to dry-and-rubbery fast. Pull it with a few moist crumbs on the pick; it firms as it cools.
The broiler goes from golden to BURNT in seconds and it is blazing hot - never walk away or check your phone. Watch the whole time and pull the instant the peaks are golden.
Blend the cottage cheese totally smooth BEFORE adding the dry ingredients - any curds left will show up as little white lumps in the finished brownie.

No marshmallows? A torched egg-white meringue is the classic stand-in - it browns under the broiler just like a marshmallow, and it's a macro UPGRADE here: fat-free AND it adds protein. A little real sugar does the structural work: it dissolves into the whites for a stable, glossy, marshmallow-like foam and is what browns under the broiler (Splenda can't brown OR build structure, so don't try to make the whole topping from it). Use granulated WHITE sugar over brown - it whips to a clean white meringue that toasts to golden tips, where brown sugar's molasses slackens the foam, starts out tan, and reads as caramel rather than marshmallow. Keep the extra sweetness as Splenda to stay lean. (If you happen to have marshmallow fluff or honey, either also works - dollop/whip in and broil.)

Built to replace the original Protein S'mores Brownies (492 cal, ~36% fat). Changes: dropped the coconut-oil drizzle, swapped the un-toasted yogurt/pudding 'marshmallow' frosting for a real broiled topping, switched to chocolate protein, and cut the batch ~in half. The marshmallow stand-in is a torched sugar-meringue (fat-free, adds protein). Lands ~17-18% fat.

New to broiling? The 'broiler' is your oven's top heating element - it fires intense heat straight DOWN to brown tops fast, like an upside-down grill. (On many gas ovens it's a pull-out drawer underneath the oven instead of a setting.) Move the rack up BEFORE you turn it on, choose the 'Broil' or 'Hi Broil' setting, and keep the door closed on a modern electric oven (only crack it if your manual says to). Use a metal pan and tuck any parchment edges down so they can't touch the element.

No broiler at all? Crank the oven to 475-500F and put the topped brownie on the top rack for 4-6 minutes, watching it the same way. Or skip toasting entirely - the meringue is still sweet and good unbrowned, just paler and without the campfire flavor.

Graham in two forms, each where it works best: CRUMBS for the base - bound with the maple and egg white they press into an even layer that cuts cleanly with the soft brownie and resists sogging - and whole-cracker SHARDS on top (optional) for the crisp snap, which only survives up top where it isn't buried in wet batter. Don't line the base with whole wafers: they crack when you slice and go soft by day two.

Reading meringue peaks: lift the beaters straight out. SOFT peaks flop over at the tip; STIFF peaks stand straight up and hold. Stiff, glossy peaks are ideal for a broiled topping - they hold the spiky swirls that brown best - but soft-to-medium peaks also work fine (made and rated excellent that way): they just spread a little flatter and brown more evenly instead of in spikes. So don't kill yourself chasing stiff, especially with pasteurized whites; just get it past the loose, ribbony stage. Whatever you reach, stop while it's still glossy - beat past that and the foam goes dry, dull and grainy and beads water in the oven.

By hand (no mixer): use a BALLOON WHISK, not a spatula - a spatula folds air out, so it can't build a meringue. The bowl and whisk must be spotlessly grease-free (metal or glass beats plastic; a speck of fat or yolk kills the foam), and room-temp whites plus the cream of tartar both help it stiffen faster. Expect about 5-8 minutes of brisk, near-continuous whisking to reach stiff peaks for this small amount - LONGER if your whites are carton/pasteurized; soft peaks arrive around 3-4 minutes, push past them. Add the real sugar gradually (dumping it all at once deflates the foam and takes longer to recover). Use a spatula or spoon only afterward, to scrape the meringue out and swirl it onto the brownie.

Egg whites: FRESH shell whites whip fastest and highest. CARTON / pasteurized whites work, but the pasteurization heat partially sets the proteins, so they whip slower, with more effort, and may not get quite as stiff - lean on the acid and be patient (the warm-bowl Swiss method helps a lot here). On acid: one pinch of cream of tartar per ~2 whites is the FULL dose - it lowers the pH so the foam forms and holds. More won't whip it faster (the holdup is mechanical) and won't taste sour at this level, but don't pile it on. Prefer dry cream of tartar over lemon juice - lemon adds water that slackens the foam; if it's all you have, a few drops is plenty.

A pinch of instant espresso (about 1/8 tsp) amplifies the cocoa so the brownie tastes MORE chocolatey, not like coffee - but keep it to a pinch. Too much tips it toward mocha/coffee. (Tested: a little over a pinch still tasted excellent, but a pinch is the target.)

steps.instructionText: Cook the pumpkin (or unsweetened applesauce - see note) in a nonstick pan over medium heat, 3-5 min, stirring, until thickened and nutty. Remove and COOL COMPLETELY (hot mix will scramble the eggs).
Blend the cottage cheese completely smooth (immersion blender or food processor) - no visible curd, or the cheesecake turns grainy.

Beat the light cream cheese alone until smooth, then add yogurt, blended cottage cheese, protein powder, sweetener, vanilla, lemon, and vanilla pudding mix (or its no-pudding swap - see note). Sift/whisk in the AP flour smooth (no lumps) and mix just until combined - don't overwork it. Warm the bowl ~15 sec if it clumps.
Add the eggs and egg white and the cooled pumpkin. Mix just until smooth - do NOT overbeat once eggs are in (air = cracks, and we want a dense set anyway).
Pour into a parchment-lined 9-inch pan. Tap on the counter to level and pop bubbles.

Bake in a WATER BATH at 300F for ~40-45 min: foil-wrap the pan bottom and up the sides (heavy-duty, doubled) so the bath can't seep in, set it inside a larger pan, and pour boiling water halfway up the sides. The gentle, humid, low heat is the anti-crack method and gives the smooth top. Time is a guide - pull on the cue: center just set with only a slight wobble (~155-160F), not visibly jiggly. It firms further as it cools; don't chase a fully dry center, that's where a lean cheesecake turns rubbery.
Cool: oven off and door cracked 10-20 min, then counter to room temp ~1-1.5 hr (max 2 hr out), then fridge at least 4 hr — overnight is best and gives the densest, firmest set. Best the next day.

notes.text: The cooked pumpkin MUST be room temp before it goes into the batter — even slightly warm pumpkin will begin cooking the eggs in s4 and leave scrambled streaks in the finished cheesecake.

Blend the cottage cheese until completely smooth — any visible curd survives baking and makes the cheesecake grainy. An immersion blender in a tall cup works well; a food processor needs 2 full minutes.

Don't overbeat once the eggs are in — mix on low just until smooth. Beating air into a lean cheesecake causes it to puff, then crack and sink as it cools, and it won't set to the dense texture this recipe is tuned for.
Pull when the center reads 155–160F or just barely wobbles — it looks underdone but firms fully overnight. Chasing a dry, fully-set center in the oven is where this lean formula turns rubbery.
The staged cool (oven door cracked → counter → fridge) prevents the sudden temperature drop that causes surface cracking. Don't skip the oven rest or move it to the fridge while still hot.

Out of vanilla SF pudding? Don't reach for a flavored pudding (butterscotch, etc.) - its flavor tints the whole cheesecake and fights a vanilla or berry batter. And you barely need it for structure here: the 2 tbsp AP flour plus the eggs already do the set, so the pudding is mostly vanilla flavor, a little sweetness, and the creamy body its gums lend. Clean swap: ~1 tbsp cornstarch (or skip it and lean on the flour) + an extra splash of vanilla (~1/4-1/2 tsp) and a pinch more Splenda to cover what the pudding carried. Macro-trivial - the recipe of record keeps the pudding; this is just the in-a-pinch swap. (A flavored pudding is only fair where its flavor matches the variant, e.g. butterscotch in the Banana Butterscotch Cheesecake.)

Swap: unsweetened applesauce works 1:1 for the pumpkin as the fat-replacing moisture/body. Reduce it the same way (cook it down until thickened) so it doesn't loosen the batter - applesauce starts wetter and, with more sugar than pumpkin, browns and scorches faster, so keep it moving and pull it a touch sooner. It reads a little sweeter and more neutral - actually cleaner under vanilla or a berry swirl, where pumpkin's faint earthiness can muddy things; keep the pumpkin for the warm/spiced variants (biscoff, butterscotch) where that earthiness helps. Macro-trivial (~+6 cal/recipe). Recipe of record keeps pumpkin; this is the in-a-pinch / flavor-preference swap.

Water bath = the smooth, crack-free top, and it's the standard bake now. Foil-wrap the pan bottom and up the sides (heavy-duty, doubled) so no water seeps into the cake or crust - a slow-cooker liner bag or silicone band is extra insurance. Start with boiling water so the oven recovers temp fast. At 300F it's gentle and slow - lean on the wobble / 155-160F cue, not the clock.

If the batter is too thick to pour and swirl cleanly, thin it with a tablespoon of unsweetened almond milk (or water) at a time until it's smooth and pourable. It bakes off - the flour, pudding, and protein keep the dense set. Cold dairy or a batter that's sat a while both stiffen it, so room-temp ingredients and mixing just before you pour help too.

payload.instructionText: Pour half the filling onto the cooled crust. Drop spoonfuls of the protein caramel swirl over it, add the rest of the filling, then drag a knife through in a few S-strokes to marble (don't overmix). Tap the pan on the counter to level and pop bubbles.

Once fully chilled (ideally overnight), lift the cake out with the parchment sling onto a plate. Warm the caramel and the ganache separately just until pourable — a few seconds; they should ribbon, not run. Drizzle both over the top in a back-and-forth criss-cross (use a spoon, or a zip-top bag with a tiny corner snipped). Finish with a pinch of flaky salt. Slice with a hot, wiped knife.

payload.text: Mix on low after adding eggs — the 2.5 scoops of vanilla protein make this batter dense and prone to aeration. Overbeating here traps air that expands in the oven, then collapses and cracks the top.

Only 2-3 lazy S-strokes with the knife to marble the butterscotch swirl — more than that and you'll fully incorporate it, losing the pockets. The swirl should still be visible as distinct veins before it goes in the oven.

Pull at the first sign of a set edge with a slight wobble in the center (~155-160F) — with 2.5 scoops of protein this filling dries out faster than a traditional cheesecake. A fully still center means it's already overdone.

For a drizzle-consistency caramel (not thick), stop as soon as the almond milk is whisked smooth (~225F) and the sauce ribbons off a spoon — it thickens significantly as it cools, so pull earlier than you think you need to.

Add the almond milk WARM — cold liquid hits the melted unsweetened baking chocolate and can seize it into a grainy clump. A few seconds in the microwave before whisking it in prevents a seized ganache.

payload.instructionText: Brown the butter: melt the butter in a light-colored pan over medium, swirling, until it foams, then smells nutty and the milk solids turn golden-amber (~2-3 min) - pull the instant it's amber, it goes from nutty to burnt in seconds. Off the heat, stir in the cinnamon plus a pinch each of ground ginger and nutmeg and let them bloom in the hot butter ~30 sec - this is where the speculoos 'cookie' flavor comes from (brown butter alone is nutty, not spiced). Scrape it all, including the toasty brown bits, into a small bowl and cool to barely warm.
Melt 15 g Biscoff 10-15 sec until pourable and drizzle it over the top of the batter. Drag a toothpick through in a few S-curves to marble it - swirl, don't stir it in.

Beat the fat-free cream cheese alone until smooth, then add the yogurt, blended cottage cheese, protein powder, powdered peanut butter, sweetener, vanilla, lemon, the 45 g Biscoff, the cooled browned-butter spice mixture, and the vanilla pudding mix. Sift/whisk in the AP flour smooth (no lumps) and mix just until combined - don't overwork it. Warm the bowl ~15 sec if it clumps.

payload.text: Brown butter goes from nutty-amber to acrid-burnt in seconds. Pull it the moment the milk solids are golden and it smells like toffee; if it smells sharp or the bits are black, start over - burnt butter taints the whole cake.

Bloom the cinnamon, ginger, and nutmeg in the hot butter off the heat - the spices are fat-soluble, so 30 sec in the browned butter wakes them up far more than stirring them into cold batter. Brown butter brings the nutty caramel depth; the bloomed spices are what make it actually read as Biscoff.

This batter is leaner than a classic cheesecake (fat-free cream cheese), so it sets firmer and dries out faster - do NOT overbake. Pull at a just-set center with a slight wobble; chase a fully firm center and it bakes out rubbery.
Swirl the melted Biscoff on top, don't stir it in - a few toothpick S-curves keep a marbled pattern. Blend it all the way in and you just muddy the color and lose the 'Biscoff cheesecake' look.

Crustless by design - the Biscoff and browned butter carry the cookie flavor without a crust's calories. If you want a crust, the Protein Graham Crust sub-recipe slots in like it does on the other cheesecakes (about +50 cal/slice).

All 55 g of Biscoff goes on top as an unbaked glaze - undiluted and never baked, so the flavor reads far stronger and the top stays glossy (baking the spread into the batter is what muddied the look and dulled the flavor before). Press the graham crumbs on while the glaze is still tacky, not after it sets, or they won't stick - a thin ring around just the rim frames the glossy top. For an on-theme version, use crushed Biscoff cookies instead of graham.

payload.instructionText: Make the swirl: simmer the mixed berries with the Splenda and cornstarch over medium heat, mashing, until jammy and thick (4-6 min). Off heat, stir in the imitation blueberry extract. Cool fully before swirling - hot jam melts streaks into the batter.

Pour about two-thirds of the batter into the parchment-lined 9-inch pan. Spoon dollops of the cooled berry swirl over it, add the rest of the batter, dollop a little more swirl on top, and drag a knife through in S-curves to marble - 3-4 passes only (over-swirling greys the batter). Tap on the counter to level and pop bubbles.

Bake in a WATER BATH at 300F (TEST): wrap the pan bottom in foil, set it inside a larger roasting pan, and pour boiling water halfway up the sides. Bake ~55-70 min until the edges are set and the center still jiggles slightly. The gentle, humid, low heat is the classic anti-crack method - if this finishes smoother and less cracked than our dry 325F bake, we roll the water bath out to the other cheesecakes.
Once fully chilled, top with a scatter of fresh or thawed mixed berries just before serving.

payload.text: Foil-wrap the pan bottom so the bath can't seep in. Water bath + 300F = slow, even set with no surface overcook, which is what prevents the dome-and-crack. This is the recipe we're using to decide whether to convert all the cheesecakes.

The imitation blueberry extract is potent - 0.5 tsp is plenty; too much reads artificial. The cornstarch keeps the swirl from weeping into the custard. Toss the topping berries in a pinch of cornstarch if they're wet.

Add the pumpkin to the same pan and cook 3-5 min, stirring, until thickened and nutty. In the last ~45-60 sec, stir the ground cinnamon into the hot fruit to toast it — it should turn fragrant and deepen a shade. Toast it in the fruit, not in a dry pan: loose ground cinnamon scorches in seconds, but the fruit's moisture buffers it so it blooms evenly. Remove and COOL COMPLETELY (hot mix will scramble the eggs).

Pour into a parchment-lined 9-inch pan. Tap on the counter to level and pop bubbles. For the topping, toast the graham crumbs with the garnish cinnamon in a dry pan over medium heat ~1 min, stirring, until fragrant, then let cool. Scatter over the cheesecake after baking so they stay crisp.
Finish with sugar-free cinnamon syrup to taste.

payload.instructionText: Brown the butter: melt the butter in a light-colored pan over medium, swirling, until it foams, then smells nutty and the milk solids turn golden-amber (~2-3 min) - pull the instant it's amber, it goes from nutty to burnt in seconds. Off the heat, stir in the cinnamon plus a pinch each of ground ginger and nutmeg and let them bloom in the hot butter ~30 sec - this is where the speculoos 'cookie' flavor comes from (brown butter alone is nutty, not spiced). Scrape it all, including the toasty brown bits, into a small bowl and cool to barely warm.
Melt 15 g Biscoff 10-15 sec until pourable and drizzle it over the top of the batter. Drag a toothpick through in a few S-curves to marble it - swirl, don't stir it in.

Beat the fat-free cream cheese alone until smooth, then add the yogurt, blended cottage cheese, protein powder, powdered peanut butter, sweetener, vanilla, lemon, the 45 g Biscoff, the cooled browned-butter spice mixture, and the vanilla pudding mix. Sift/whisk in the AP flour smooth (no lumps) and mix just until combined - don't overwork it. Warm the bowl ~15 sec if it clumps.

payload.text: Brown butter goes from nutty-amber to acrid-burnt in seconds. Pull it the moment the milk solids are golden and it smells like toffee; if it smells sharp or the bits are black, start over - burnt butter taints the whole cake.

Bloom the cinnamon, ginger, and nutmeg in the hot butter off the heat - the spices are fat-soluble, so 30 sec in the browned butter wakes them up far more than stirring them into cold batter. Brown butter brings the nutty caramel depth; the bloomed spices are what make it actually read as Biscoff.

This batter is leaner than a classic cheesecake (fat-free cream cheese), so it sets firmer and dries out faster - do NOT overbake. Pull at a just-set center with a slight wobble; chase a fully firm center and it bakes out rubbery.
Swirl the melted Biscoff on top, don't stir it in - a few toothpick S-curves keep a marbled pattern. Blend it all the way in and you just muddy the color and lose the 'Biscoff cheesecake' look.

Crustless by design - the Biscoff and browned butter carry the cookie flavor without a crust's calories. If you want a crust, the Protein Graham Crust sub-recipe slots in like it does on the other cheesecakes (about +50 cal/slice).

The imitation blueberry extract is potent - 0.5 tsp is plenty; too much reads artificial. The cornstarch keeps the swirl from weeping into the custard. Toss the topping berries in a pinch of cornstarch if they're wet.

payload.instructionText: Toast 65 g shredded coconut in a dry skillet over medium heat, 3-5 min, stirring, until golden and fragrant (it colors fast then burns - watch it). Cool. Grind 45 g to a fine meal (spice grinder or food processor) and beat it into the filling with the wet ingredients in step 3 so the coconut disperses throughout; reserve the other 20 g for the topping.
Once the cheesecake is fully chilled, scatter the reserved 20 g toasted coconut evenly over the top just before serving (keeps it crisp).

Grind the 45 g filling coconut to a fine meal (spice grinder, 15–20 sec) before beating it in — coarse shreds leave sandy pockets; a fine meal disperses evenly and gives a smooth coconut flavor throughout every bite.

Pull at 155–160F center or when there's only a slight wobble in the middle — chasing a fully set center with 2 scoops of protein powder and cottage cheese will result in a dry, rubbery slice. It firms dramatically overnight in the fridge.

Pipe or dollop the yogurt cream over the chocolate spread, then drag a toothpick through both for a marbled swirl. Chill 15-20 min to set the spread before slicing.
Spread the prepared Low-Cal Chocolate Spread (sub-recipe) in a thin even layer over the chilled, set cheesecake.
Pipe the yogurt cream into small decorative spiral swirls (rosettes) across the top as the final finish. Chill 15-20 min to set the spread before slicing.
Press the chocolate graham crust firmly and evenly into the bottom of the parchment-lined pan; chill while you make the filling.
Pour the batter over the chilled chocolate graham crust in the lined pan. Tap on the counter to level and pop bubbles.

Bake in a WATER BATH at 300F for 45-55 min: foil-wrap the pan bottom and up the sides (heavy-duty, doubled) so the bath can't seep in, set it inside a larger pan, and pour boiling water halfway up the sides. The gentle, humid, low heat is the anti-crack method and gives the smooth top. Time is a guide - pull on the cue: center just set with only a slight wobble (~155-160F), not visibly jiggly. It firms further as it cools; don't chase a fully dry center, that's where a lean cheesecake turns rubbery.

steps.instructionText: Cook the pumpkin (or unsweetened applesauce - see note) in a nonstick pan over medium heat, 3-5 min, stirring, until thickened and nutty. Remove and COOL COMPLETELY (hot mix will scramble the eggs).
Blend the cottage cheese completely smooth (immersion blender or food processor) - no visible curd, or the cheesecake turns grainy.

Beat the light cream cheese alone until smooth, then add yogurt, blended cottage cheese, chocolate protein powder, sweetener, vanilla, and lemon. Sift/whisk in the cocoa, cornstarch, and AP flour smooth (no lumps) and mix just until combined - don't overwork it. Warm the bowl ~15 sec if it clumps.
Add the eggs and egg white and the cooled pumpkin. Mix just until smooth - do NOT overbeat once eggs are in (air = cracks, and we want a dense set anyway).
Pour the batter over the chilled chocolate graham crust in the lined pan. Tap on the counter to level and pop bubbles.

Bake in a WATER BATH at 300F for 45-55 min: foil-wrap the pan bottom and up the sides (heavy-duty, doubled) so the bath can't seep in, set it inside a larger pan, and pour boiling water halfway up the sides. The gentle, humid, low heat is the anti-crack method and gives the smooth top. Time is a guide - pull on the cue: center just set with only a slight wobble (~155-160F), not visibly jiggly. It firms further as it cools; don't chase a fully dry center, that's where a lean cheesecake turns rubbery.
Cool: oven off and door cracked 10-20 min, then counter to room temp ~1-1.5 hr (max 2 hr out), then fridge at least 4 hr — overnight is best and gives the densest, firmest set. Best the next day.
Spread the prepared Low-Cal Chocolate Spread (sub-recipe) in a thin even layer over the chilled, set cheesecake.
Press the chocolate graham crust firmly and evenly into the bottom of the parchment-lined pan; chill while you make the filling.

notes.text: The cooked pumpkin MUST be room temp before it goes into the batter — even slightly warm pumpkin will begin cooking the eggs in s4 and leave scrambled streaks in the finished cheesecake.

Blend the cottage cheese until completely smooth — any visible curd survives baking and makes the cheesecake grainy. An immersion blender in a tall cup works well; a food processor needs 2 full minutes.

Don't overbeat once the eggs are in — mix on low just until smooth. Beating air into a lean cheesecake causes it to puff, then crack and sink as it cools, and it won't set to the dense texture this recipe is tuned for.
Pull when the center reads 155–160F or just barely wobbles — it looks underdone but firms fully overnight. Chasing a dry, fully-set center in the oven is where this lean formula turns rubbery.
The staged cool (oven door cracked → counter → fridge) prevents the sudden temperature drop that causes surface cracking. Don't skip the oven rest or move it to the fridge while still hot.

Out of vanilla SF pudding? Don't reach for a flavored pudding (butterscotch, etc.) - its flavor tints the whole cheesecake and fights a vanilla or berry batter. And you barely need it for structure here: the 2 tbsp AP flour plus the eggs already do the set, so the pudding is mostly vanilla flavor, a little sweetness, and the creamy body its gums lend. Clean swap: ~1 tbsp cornstarch (or skip it and lean on the flour) + an extra splash of vanilla (~1/4-1/2 tsp) and a pinch more Splenda to cover what the pudding carried. Macro-trivial - the recipe of record keeps the pudding; this is just the in-a-pinch swap. (A flavored pudding is only fair where its flavor matches the variant, e.g. butterscotch in the Banana Butterscotch Cheesecake.)

Swap: unsweetened applesauce works 1:1 for the pumpkin as the fat-replacing moisture/body. Reduce it the same way (cook it down until thickened) so it doesn't loosen the batter - applesauce starts wetter and, with more sugar than pumpkin, browns and scorches faster, so keep it moving and pull it a touch sooner. It reads a little sweeter and more neutral - actually cleaner under vanilla or a berry swirl, where pumpkin's faint earthiness can muddy things; keep the pumpkin for the warm/spiced variants (biscoff, butterscotch) where that earthiness helps. Macro-trivial (~+6 cal/recipe). Recipe of record keeps pumpkin; this is the in-a-pinch / flavor-preference swap.

Water bath = the smooth, crack-free top, and it's the standard bake now. Foil-wrap the pan bottom and up the sides (heavy-duty, doubled) so no water seeps into the cake or crust - a slow-cooker liner bag or silicone band is extra insurance. Start with boiling water so the oven recovers temp fast. At 300F it's gentle and slow - lean on the wobble / 155-160F cue, not the clock.

If the batter is too thick to pour and swirl cleanly, thin it with a tablespoon of unsweetened almond milk (or water) at a time until it's smooth and pourable. It bakes off - the flour, pudding, and protein keep the dense set. Cold dairy or a batter that's sat a while both stiffen it, so room-temp ingredients and mixing just before you pour help too.

6eb4862c-f5a4-49c9-abf1-b70c48c779d9.name: Chocolate Protein Donut Holes
6eb4862c-f5a4-49c9-abf1-b70c48c779d9.description: Glazed chocolate protein timbits, synthesized from three source recipes (a 45-ball cookies&cream air-fryer dough, a 26-ball oxywhey air-fryer dough, and an 8-ball baked egg+pudding dough). Best-of: the EGG + SF pudding from the baked version (the anti-rubber, anti-dry levers - fat for tenderness, gums to hold moisture), the real cocoa level + Greek-yogurt body + quick air-fry from the air-fryer versions (chocolatey and hard to overbake), AP flour + baking powder instead of drying coconut flour, and just ONE scoop of protein (two scoops is what turns these rubbery - more protein powder is NOT free here). Chocolate protein (out of vanilla). The glaze is the point: no powdered-sugar sub on hand, so granulated Splenda is blitzed to a powder for body, a little melted semi-sweet chocolate gives gloss and lets it actually SET in the fridge, and liquid monk fruit + a pinch of salt + espresso powder are the kick - concentrated sweetness and deepened chocolate with no grit. ~16 balls, very low fat/ball, high protein.
6eb4862c-f5a4-49c9-abf1-b70c48c779d9.author: user

steps.instructionText: Whisk together the dry ingredients: AP flour, chocolate protein powder, cocoa, SF vanilla pudding mix, baking powder (1 tsp), granulated Splenda, and a pinch of salt.
Add the Greek yogurt and the whole egg; stir and fold to a soft, slightly sticky dough. Chill 15-20 min until it firms up enough to handle (protein/yogurt dough is sticky warm).
Roll into ~16 even balls with damp or lightly cocoa-dusted hands.

Air fry at 350F for ~5-6 min (or bake at 350F for 10-12 min) until just set and springy to a light press. Pull them the moment they spring back - do NOT chase a dry center, that's where they turn rubbery. Cool ~10 min.

Glaze: blitz the granulated Splenda to a fine powder in a blender or spice grinder (this is your DIY powdered sweetener - the body of the glaze). Separately, melt the semi-sweet chocolate chips in short microwave bursts, stirring, until just smooth.

Whisk the melted chocolate with the powdered Splenda, cocoa, almond milk, liquid monk fruit, vanilla, espresso powder, and a pinch of salt into a smooth, pourable glaze. Thin with a few more drops of almond milk if it's too thick to coat. Taste and add a drop more monk fruit if you want more kick.

Dip or toss the balls in the glaze while they're warm but NOT hot (warm grabs the glaze; hot makes it slide right off). Set on a wire rack and chill to set the glaze - the melted chocolate firms it into a real coating. Expect about half the glaze to drip off; that's normal.

notes.text: Overbaking is the #1 thing that ruins these. Protein-powder + Greek-yogurt dough goes rubbery and dry the second it overcooks. Air fryers run hot and fast - start checking at 5 min and pull the moment they spring back to a light press; the center can look slightly underdone and it'll be perfect once cooled.

The egg, the SF pudding mix, and holding protein to ONE scoop are the anti-rubber levers. Don't 'boost the macros' by adding a second scoop - extra whey is exactly what makes protein bakes dry and bouncy. If you want more protein in the day, eat two donut holes, don't load the dough.

No powdered-sugar sub on hand? Blitz the granulated Splenda to a fine powder in a blender or spice grinder - that powder is what gives the glaze body and a smooth (not grainy) coat. The little bit of melted semi-sweet chocolate is what makes it glossy and lets it SET in the fridge into a real shell instead of a wet smear.

The glaze kick comes from concentration, not sugar: liquid monk fruit dials sweetness up with zero grit, a pinch of salt sharpens it, and the espresso powder deepens the chocolate (you won't taste coffee at 1/8 tsp). Build the glaze, then taste and add monk fruit a drop at a time until it pops.
Chill the dough 15-20 min before rolling - warm protein/yogurt dough is sticky and won't ball up cleanly. Damp or lightly cocoa-dusted hands keep it from gluing to you.

801a948a-f777-43a1-a101-f06cd3655105.description: A pure sweet white glaze for protein timbits/donut holes - the classic thin sugar glaze, made without powdered sugar. No powdered-sugar sub on hand, so granulated Splenda is blitzed to a fine powder for the body, loosened with almond milk, and the kick comes from liquid monk fruit + a pinch of salt + vanilla (concentrated sweetness with no grit). Deliberately FLAVOR-NEUTRAL so it works as the glaze on any timbit flavor - the chocolate (or whatever) lives in the timbit, the glaze is just clean sweet shine. Reusable sub-recipe. 1 batch glazes ~16 timbits.

steps.instructionText: Blitz the granulated Splenda to a fine powder in a blender or spice grinder - this is your DIY powdered sweetener and the body of the glaze. (Granulated sweetener won't dissolve smooth; powdering it is what gives a clean, non-grainy coat.)

Whisk the powdered Splenda with the almond milk, vanilla, liquid monk fruit, and a pinch of salt until smooth and just pourable - it should ribbon off the whisk and coat the back of a spoon. Add almond milk a few drops at a time if too thick. Taste and add monk fruit a drop at a time until the sweetness pops.

notes.text: Powdered sweetener glaze sets softer than a real powdered-sugar glaze - it firms as it dries on a rack and firms more in the fridge, but it stays a thin glaze, not a hard crackable shell. Keep it on the thicker side (less almond milk) and let it dry undisturbed for the best set.

The kick is concentration, not bulk: liquid monk fruit pushes sweetness up with zero grit, and a pinch of salt sharpens it so it reads like a real sugar glaze instead of flat diet-sweet. Always finish by tasting and adjusting the monk fruit.

Flavor-neutral on purpose. To theme it to a flavor without breaking the all-timbit reusability, swap the vanilla for another extract (maple, almond, peppermint) - but for chocolate timbits leave it plain vanilla so the glaze stays the clean sweet contrast to the chocolate.

53e58375-f874-40f2-8380-2e4b0accdabd.commitMessage: half-sugar real glaze: granulated sugar + cornstarch (DIY powdered sugar) + monk fruit; sets a real crust; air-dry not fridge

steps.instructionText: Blitz the granulated sugar with the cornstarch to a fine powder in a blender or spice grinder - this is DIY powdered sugar. The cornstarch keeps it from caking and gives the glaze body; sift out any grit.

Whisk the powdered sugar with just enough warm milk to make a THICK, barely-pourable glaze - start with 1 tbsp and add by the teaspoon; a thin glaze won't crust. Whisk in the liquid monk fruit, vanilla, and a pinch of salt. For the best set, warm it ~10-15 sec and stir until the sugar is fully dissolved and smooth - dissolved sugar re-crystallizes into a cleaner crust as it dries. Taste and add monk fruit a drop at a time for sweetness.

notes.text: This is a real (half-quantity) sugar glaze, so it actually crusts like a donut-shop glaze - but only if you dry it right: dip the timbits warm, then AIR-DRY on a rack at room temp. Do NOT refrigerate it - cold and damp keep it tacky and kill the crust. It skins over in ~15-20 min; for a thicker Tim-Hortons-style shell, double-dip (glaze, let set, glaze again).

Half the sugar of a full glaze, with liquid monk fruit carrying the rest of the sweetness - that keeps it light (fat-free carbs, ~half the sugar) while still giving a real sugar crust. Don't replace the missing sugar with granulated Splenda: it's maltodextrin-based and hygroscopic, which actively fights the crust you're after. Sugar sets; monk fruit sweetens.

Flavor-neutral on purpose. To theme it to a flavor without breaking the all-timbit reusability, swap the vanilla for another extract (maple, almond, peppermint) - but for chocolate timbits leave it plain vanilla so the glaze stays the clean sweet contrast to the chocolate.

White granulated sugar gives the cleanest clear-white TH look. Brown sugar works at the same weight but tints the glaze tan and adds a light caramel note - not classic, but honestly nice on a chocolate timbit. Powder it the same way (it may clump from the molasses - sift well).

steps.instructionText: Blitz the brown sugar with the cornstarch to a fine powder in a blender or spice grinder - this is DIY powdered (brown) sugar; the cornstarch keeps it from caking and gives the glaze body. Brown sugar is moist and may clump - sift out lumps, or just skip the blitz and dissolve it fully in the warm-milk step instead.

Whisk the powdered sugar with just enough warm milk to make a THICK, barely-pourable glaze - start with 1 tbsp and add by the teaspoon; a thin glaze won't crust. Whisk in the liquid monk fruit, vanilla, and a pinch of salt. For the best set, warm it ~10-15 sec and stir until the sugar is fully dissolved and smooth - dissolved sugar re-crystallizes into a cleaner crust as it dries. Taste and add monk fruit a drop at a time for sweetness.

notes.text: This is a real (half-quantity) sugar glaze, so it actually crusts like a donut-shop glaze - but only if you dry it right: dip the timbits warm, then AIR-DRY on a rack at room temp. Do NOT refrigerate it - cold and damp keep it tacky and kill the crust. It skins over in ~15-20 min; for a thicker Tim-Hortons-style shell, double-dip (glaze, let set, glaze again).

Half the sugar of a full glaze, with liquid monk fruit carrying the rest of the sweetness - that keeps it light (fat-free carbs, ~half the sugar) while still giving a real sugar crust. Don't replace the missing sugar with granulated Splenda: it's maltodextrin-based and hygroscopic, which actively fights the crust you're after. Sugar sets; monk fruit sweetens.

Flavor-neutral on purpose. To theme it to a flavor without breaking the all-timbit reusability, swap the vanilla for another extract (maple, almond, peppermint) - but for chocolate timbits leave it plain vanilla so the glaze stays the clean sweet contrast to the chocolate.

Brown sugar is the default here - on taste, its molasses caramel note plays beautifully with a chocolate timbit (and most flavors). Swap in white granulated sugar at the same weight for a cleaner, clear-white, flavor-neutral glaze (e.g. under a fruit or vanilla timbit where caramel would muddy it). Same set either way.

notes.text: NO protein powder, on purpose. Whey denaturing in the batter is exactly what made every protein-brownie base bouncy and dry. This base gets dense/fudgy from real fat + low flour instead; don't add a scoop to 'fix' the macros - that recreates the rubber problem. Protein here is ~16g/batch from the egg + yogurt.

Brown sugar is the chew lever - fudgy comes from fat, dense from low flour, but CHEWY comes from dissolved sugar, and molasses adds moisture plus a caramel note against the chocolate. The Splenda tops off sweetness without more calories. If the chew still falls short, shift the ratio toward brown sugar (each extra tbsp ~ +45 cal/batch) before touching anything else.

Overbaking is the killer - with only ~31g flour there is no structure to save a dry bake. Pull at moist crumbs on the toothpick, never clean, and let them set as they cool. Fudgy brownies always look slightly underdone hot.
Fat runs ~35-40% of calories - deliberate. The batch's ~25g of fat (butter + chips + egg) IS the fudge; this is filed as a lean dessert (high carb, low cal, satiating), not a protein bake.

No baking soda, on purpose - lift is the enemy of dense. The yogurt's acidity would have reacted with soda and aerated the crumb; without it the batter sets as a tight fudge slab. Priority for this base is FUDGY + DENSE first, chew second.
